ch01.anchor: a history of the Central Special Branch begins with stage magic
ch01.note: The Central Special Branch (Zhongyang Teke) was the Chinese Communist Party’s first professional intelligence and security service, set up in Shanghai in 1927–28 under Zhou Enlai and active until 1935. Divided into sections for general affairs, intelligence, action (the “Red Squad”), and radio communications, it shielded the Party’s underground leadership, planted agents inside the Kuomintang police and secret services, punished traitors, and built the Party’s first clandestine wireless network. Western scholarship (Frederic Wakeman, Policing Shanghai, 1927–1937) treats it as the seed of all later Chinese Communist intelligence work.

ch01.anchor: He was Gu Shunzhang.
ch01.note: Gu Shunzhang (1903–1935), a Shanghai labor organizer who commanded the workers’ pickets in the armed uprising of 1927, trained in political security in the Soviet Union, and was chosen by Zhou Enlai to head the Central Special Branch. A gifted amateur magician, he used stage conjuring as cover. Arrested by the Kuomintang in Wuhan in April 1931—recognized, it is said, while performing—he defected at once and betrayed the Shanghai underground, forcing a wholesale evacuation of the Party’s leaders; in reprisal the Special Branch killed members of his family. He was executed by the Kuomintang in 1935. His defection is the hinge of this book. (Corroborated: Wakeman, Policing Shanghai; Chinese and English reference works.)

ch01.anchor: "Let those above favor a thing, and those below will carry it further."
ch01.note: A saying from the Mencius (“Teng Wen Gong,” part I): where those above have a preference, those below will have it to a still greater degree. The author uses it to explain how the Empress Dowager Cixi’s taste for Western magic spread the fashion downward.

ch01.anchor: the patronage of the Western Empress Dowager
ch01.note: The Empress Dowager Cixi (1835–1908), called the “Western Empress Dowager” (Xitaihou) after the palace she occupied, was the effective ruler of China through the last half-century of the Qing dynasty. “The last years of the Guangxu reign” are the first decade of the 1900s.

ch01.anchor: the rapid-fire patter of the *guankou*
ch01.note: Guankou is the unbroken, tongue-twisting “patter” of xiangsheng (“crosstalk”), the paired comic dialogue central to northern Chinese variety art; Ma Sanli (1914–2003) was its most celebrated modern master. Wuqiao county, in Cangzhou (Hebei), is the traditional cradle of Chinese acrobatics and conjuring, and “Ghost-Hand” Wang Baohe (1944–2016) a famous latter-day sleight-of-hand performer there. The titles in quotation marks are traditional set pieces of magic and patter.

ch01.anchor: Ruan Lingyu, the tragic queen of the silent era
ch01.note: Ruan Lingyu (1910–1935), one of the great stars of the Chinese silent screen, famed for tragic roles; her suicide at twenty-four, hounded by scandal, became a national sensation. “Butterfly Wu” is Hu Die (1908–1989), the other reigning film queen of the age. Zhang Daimin, named here, was Ruan’s common-law husband, whose lawsuits against her helped drive her to her death.

ch01.anchor: the embroiderings of Frederic Wakeman
ch01.note: Frederic E. Wakeman Jr. (1937–2006), Chinese name Wei Feide, was a leading American historian of China; his Policing Shanghai, 1927–1937 (1995) and Spymaster: Dai Li and the Chinese Secret Service (2003) are standard works on the intelligence world of this book. The author lists him (with a 2011 date, apparently a Chinese edition) among writers he thinks have inflated Gu Shunzhang’s reputation as a magician.

ch01.anchor: Zhang Guotao, 1991
ch01.note: Zhang Guotao (1897–1979) was a founder of the Chinese Communist Party and one of its most senior leaders until, having lost his power struggle with Mao, he defected to the Kuomintang in 1938; he died in Canada. His memoir, My Recollections, is much cited and much distrusted.

ch01.anchor: keeps clear of the melon patch and the plum tree
ch01.note: A classical caution (guatian lixia): one does not stoop to tie a shoe in a melon patch, nor reach up to one’s hat under a plum tree, lest one be taken for a thief—that is, one avoids even the appearance of wrongdoing.

ch01.anchor: so said Yu Zecheng.
ch01.note: Yu Zecheng is the fictional Communist mole at the center of Lurk (Qianfu), a hugely popular 2009 Chinese television spy drama; his peasant “wife” and the mercenary informer Xie Ruolin, both invoked later in this chapter, are characters from it too. The author sets a line of screen dialogue beside a maxim commonly attributed to Lenin, “the enemy never sleeps.”

ch01.anchor: The Central Special Branch had another man of resource: Chen Geng.
ch01.note: Chen Geng (1903–1961) was among the most storied figures of the Chinese Communist movement: a graduate of the first class of the Whampoa Military Academy who, during the Eastern Expeditions of 1925, personally carried his stricken commandant Chiang Kai-shek to safety. Under the alias Wang Yong he ran the intelligence (Second) Section of the Central Special Branch from 1928 to 1931. He went on to become one of the People’s Liberation Army’s ablest generals, commanded the celebrated 386th Brigade against Japan, advised the Viet Minh in 1950, and served as a deputy chief of the general staff. Much of what follows draws on his posthumously published diary and autobiography.

ch01.anchor: At the Nanchang rupture I went to Wuhan
ch01.note: The source reads “the Nanchang rupture” (Nanchang jielie). Chronologically Chen Geng reached Wuhan in the spring of 1927, before the August Nanchang Uprising named just below; the phrase seems to telescope the collapse of the Kuomintang–Communist united front that year. Rendered as printed.

ch01.anchor: the Whampoa Military Academy
ch01.note: The Whampoa (Huangpu) Military Academy, founded near Guangzhou in 1924 under the first Kuomintang–Communist alliance—Chiang Kai-shek as commandant, Zhou Enlai heading its political department—trained the officer corps of both parties. Its “first class” produced a remarkable roll of commanders who would later face one another across the civil war.

ch01.anchor: After the split between the Kuomintang and the Communists I joined the Nanchang Uprising.
ch01.note: The Nanchang Uprising of August 1, 1927—the Communists’ first armed revolt after the Kuomintang turned on them—is reckoned the founding day of the Red Army, later the People’s Liberation Army. Its forces were beaten within weeks and scattered south through Huichang and the Chaozhou–Shantou region, as Chen Geng’s account describes.

ch01.anchor: Xu Enzeng — in his time chief
ch01.note: Xu Enzeng (1898–1985) ran the Kuomintang’s civilian secret service, the Central Bureau of Investigation and Statistics (Zhongtong), through the 1930s. A U.S.-trained engineer and a kinsman of the Chen brothers, he was the unwitting employer of Qian Zhuangfei—the Communist mole in his own office whose warning, after Gu Shunzhang’s 1931 defection, saved the Party’s Shanghai leadership.

ch01.anchor: Dong Jianwu was a Chinese Communist agent
ch01.note: Dong Jianwu (1891–1970), the “Red Pastor,” was an ordained Anglican clergyman and Communist agent who used St. Peter’s Church in Shanghai as a safe house and meeting place. In 1936 he escorted Mao Zedong’s two young sons abroad, and he helped arrange the American journalist Edgar Snow’s journey to the Communist base. Persecuted in the Cultural Revolution, he was rehabilitated after his death.

ch01.anchor: through the ten years of turmoil
ch01.note: “The ten years of turmoil” is the standard Chinese phrase for the Cultural Revolution (1966–76), during which many veteran Communists—especially those with pre-1949 underground or foreign connections—were persecuted as suspected traitors or spies.

ch01.anchor: "Of the two ranks one soldier left, shouldering his spear, wandering alone."
ch01.note: From Lu Xun’s quatrain inscribed on his story collection Panghuang (Wandering, 1926): “A lonely new garden of letters, a quiet old battlefield; / of the space between, one soldier left, shouldering his spear, wandering alone.” The source text prints “of the two ranks” (liang zhen) where Lu Xun wrote “of the space between” (liang jian); rendered here as printed.

ch01.anchor: when Yang Du's widow came under attack
ch01.note: Yang Du (1874–1931) was among the most brilliant and mercurial figures of the early Republic: a monarchist theorist who led the Chou’an Society in urging Yuan Shikai to take the throne in 1915. Disgraced when that failed, he turned leftward and—as Zhou Enlai revealed only in 1975—secretly joined the Chinese Communist Party in his last years, passing intelligence from within Du Yuesheng’s circle. The secret-membership claim rests on Zhou’s own testimony and Party records.

ch01.anchor: threw himself into the effort to save Li Dazhao when Li was arrested and jailed
ch01.note: Li Dazhao (1889–1927), head librarian of Peking University and, with Chen Duxiu, co-founder of the Chinese Communist Party; he led its northern organization until the warlord Zhang Zuolin had him seized from the Soviet embassy and hanged in April 1927—one of the Party’s foundational martyrdoms.

ch01.anchor: the Shanghai "notable" Du Yuesheng
ch01.note: Du Yuesheng (1888–1951), paramount boss of Shanghai’s Green Gang, was at once opium magnate, financier, philanthropist, and political fixer. He had helped Chiang Kai-shek massacre the Communists in April 1927; yet his web of connections made his household a prize for Communist intelligence, as here.

ch01.anchor: Some say Yang Du joined the Party
ch01.note: Pan Hannian (1906–1977) succeeded Chen Geng in the Party’s intelligence work and became its foremost spymaster of the 1930s and 1940s. In 1955 he was secretly arrested and, in a notorious miscarriage of justice, imprisoned for “counter-revolution” over a wartime meeting with Wang Jingwei; he died in disgrace and was posthumously cleared in 1982. His fall pulled down many he had run, including Mei Gongbin.

ch01.anchor: Pan Hannian brought Shen Duanxian — Xia Yan
ch01.note: Xia Yan (1900–1995), pen name of Shen Duanxian, was a leading left-wing playwright and screenwriter, later a senior cultural official, and in these years an underground Party member active in Shanghai intelligence and the film world.

ch01.anchor: Chen Duxiu was General Secretary
ch01.note: Chen Duxiu (1879–1942), a founder and the first General Secretary of the Chinese Communist Party and a leading light of the New Culture Movement. Blamed for the catastrophe of 1927 and later expelled as a “Trotskyist,” he died out of favor.

ch01.anchor: the poem the late Ho Chi Minh, Chairman of the Vietnam Workers' Party, gave him
ch01.note: Ho Chi Minh (1890–1969), the Vietnamese revolutionary leader, had known Chen Geng in Canton in the 1920s; in 1950 Chen Geng served as a Chinese military adviser to the Viet Minh in the Border Campaign against the French. The couplet—“In the jumbled hills a lofty scholar lies; out of the deep dense woods a hero comes”—gives this section its title.

ch01.anchor: Chen Geng's years underground began with the failure of the Great Revolution.
ch01.note: The “Great Revolution” is the Chinese name for the Nationalist–Communist alliance and Northern Expedition of 1924–27. It “failed,” from the Communist standpoint, when Chiang Kai-shek turned on his allies in the coup of April 12, 1927 and the nationwide purge that followed—the White Terror this section recounts.

ch01.anchor: The "party purge" was a movement of reverse selection within the Kuomintang
ch01.note: The “party purge” (qingdang, “party purification”) was the Kuomintang’s violent expulsion of Communists and the left from its ranks, beginning in April 1927. The casualties the author cites—some 310,000 killed—are drawn from the Communist Party’s own Sixth Congress (1928) and run well above most independent estimates; they are best read as the Party’s own reckoning of its losses.

ch01.anchor: even Chen Lifu was sick at heart
ch01.note: Chen Lifu (1900–2001), with his brother Chen Guofu, led the “CC Clique” that controlled the Kuomintang’s party machine and its Zhongtong secret service. His memoir is quoted here against his own side.

ch01.anchor: the leaders of the "February Seventh" great strike
ch01.note: The railway workers’ strike on the Beijing–Hankou line was crushed by the warlord Wu Peifu on February 7, 1923; the union leaders Lin Xiangqian and Shi Yang were executed. It became a martyrs’ touchstone of the early labor movement.

ch01.anchor: the "August Seventh" Conference
ch01.note: The emergency conference of August 7, 1927, held secretly in Hankou, ended Chen Duxiu’s leadership, set the Party on the path of armed insurrection and land revolution, and raised Qu Qiubai to its head.

ch01.anchor: the arrest of Chen Yannian
ch01.note: Chen Yannian (1898–1927), eldest son of Chen Duxiu and secretary of the Party’s Jiangsu committee, was arrested and executed in Shanghai in 1927. Zhao Shiyan (1901–1927), named just after, was another leading organizer executed the same year; both are canonical martyrs.

ch01.anchor: Qu Qiubai presided over the enlarged meeting
ch01.note: Qu Qiubai (1899–1935), writer, critic, and Party leader who headed the Communist Party after the August 1927 conference. Captured by the Kuomintang, he was executed in 1935; his prison essay Superfluous Words has made him a contested figure ever since.

ch01.anchor: Li Qiang — a Special Branch veteran
ch01.note: Li Qiang (1905–1996) built the Party’s first clandestine radio transmitter and its early ciphers in Shanghai. After 1949 he served as Minister of Foreign Trade. His firsthand testimony, quoted at length here, is a principal source on the Special Branch’s origins—including his insistence that its true name was the “Special Branch,” not a “Special Affairs Bureau.”

ch01.anchor: the head of the Soviet advisory group, Borodin
ch01.note: Mikhail Borodin (1884–1951), the Comintern’s chief political adviser to Sun Yat-sen’s Kuomintang from 1923; when the alliance broke in July 1927 he left China through the northwest. He later perished in Stalin’s camps.

ch01.anchor: When the Wang Jingwei clique
ch01.note: Wang Jingwei (1883–1944), once Sun Yat-sen’s heir apparent and leader of the Kuomintang “left,” headed the Wuhan government that broke with the Communists in July 1927 (the “separation from the Communists”). He is chiefly remembered now for later heading a Japanese-sponsored puppet regime, 1940–44.

ch01.anchor: The man was Mei Baoji.
ch01.note: Mei Baoji (1881–1947), a veteran of the 1911 Wuchang Uprising and a Republican parliamentarian, is honored in Party accounts as the first intelligence source the Communists ever ran (from 1927, on Japan). The long biography that follows is the author’s defense of him as a man of principle rather than a paid informer.

ch01.anchor: on the night of October 10 took the viceroy's yamen
ch01.note: The Wuchang Uprising of October 10, 1911—still marked as “Double Ten,” the national day of the Republic of China—set off the revolution that ended the Qing dynasty. The accidental bomb blast in the Russian concession the day before, described just above, forced the rebels’ hand.

ch01.anchor: joined their names to form the "Chou'an Society,"
ch01.note: The Chou’an Society (“Society to Plan for Stability”), formed in 1915, was the pressure group—its “six gentlemen” led by Yang Du—that campaigned to make Yuan Shikai emperor. Among its lights were the translator and thinker Yan Fu and the classicist Liu Shipei, both named here.

ch01.anchor: Mei Baoji's nephew Mei Gongbin
ch01.note: Mei Gongbin (1901–1975) spent decades as a secret Communist buried inside the Kuomintang and the “third-force” democratic parties, helping to found the Revolutionary Committee of the Kuomintang. Arrested in 1955 in the Pan Hannian affair, he was cleared only after his death; his true Party membership was disclosed at his 1980 memorial.

ch01.anchor: our Party and the Nineteenth Route Army
ch01.note: The Nineteenth Route Army won fame for its stubborn defense of Shanghai against the Japanese in early 1932. In November 1933 its generals—Li Jishen, Chen Mingshu, Cai Tingkai and others—revolted against Chiang Kai-shek and set up a short-lived “People’s Government” in Fujian, the “Fujian Incident,” which collapsed within two months.

ch01.anchor: with Song Qingling elected honorary chair
ch01.note: Song Qingling (1893–1981), widow of Sun Yat-sen, was the most eminent left-leaning figure of the Republic and a protector of the Communist underground; she later served as a vice-chair, and honorary president, of the People’s Republic.

ch01.anchor: "The rain has passed, yet the fragrance lingers; such purity is not soon forgotten."
ch01.note: The couplet, by the Macau businessman and statesman Ma Man Kei (1919–2014), gives this section its title; its second line, gaojie zi nanwang—“such purity is not soon forgotten”—is the phrase rendered in the heading.

ch01.anchor: This was the "May Thirtieth" massacre that shook China and the world
ch01.note: On May 30, 1925, British-officered police of the International Settlement fired on a student demonstration on Nanjing Road, killing about a dozen. The outrage set off the nationwide May Thirtieth Movement of strikes and boycotts—a decisive surge of Chinese anti-imperialism and a making of the early labor movement.

ch01.anchor: we stored the four at Shen Yanbing's home
ch01.note: Shen Yanbing (1896–1981) is far better known by his pen name, Mao Dun, the great novelist of Midnight. In these years he was an underground Communist, and—as here—lent his home to the Party’s work.

ch01.anchor: Yan Karlovich Berzin
ch01.note: Jan Berzin (1889–1938), a Latvian-born Bolshevik, headed Soviet military intelligence (the Fourth Department, later the GRU) from 1924 to 1935 and oversaw the Moscow training of Chinese agents, Gu Shunzhang and Chen Geng among them. He was shot in Stalin’s purges.

ch01.anchor: on the model of the Soviet State Political Directorate
ch01.note: The State Political Directorate (GPU/OGPU) was the Soviet political police and intelligence service, forerunner of the KGB; the Russian historian’s point is that the Special Branch’s counter-espionage committee was built to this model.

ch01.anchor: The man who "faced heaven and laughed, the blade at his own throat"
ch01.note: From the death-cell poem of Tan Sitong (1865–1898), the reformer beheaded after the failed Hundred Days’ Reform: “I face heaven and laugh, the blade at my throat; / I leave behind two hearts, bold as the peaks of Kunlun.” He is the archetype of the martyr who welcomes death for a cause.

ch01.anchor: "carries a twig in his beak to the end of time in a body but an inch long."
ch01.note: An allusion to the myth of the Jingwei bird: a drowned girl reborn as a small bird that carries twigs and pebbles forever, trying to fill the sea that killed her—the emblem of tireless, seemingly hopeless devotion.

ch01.anchor: *Qui nescit dissimulare, nescit vivere*
ch01.note: “He who does not know how to dissimulate does not know how to live”—a maxim of Renaissance statecraft long linked to Louis XI of France. Its sense supplies this chapter’s title, “No Concealment, No Survival.”

ch01.anchor: Li Dazhao and Fang Zhimin were such models
ch01.note: A roll of canonical Communist martyrs: Fang Zhimin (1899–1935), leader of the Jiangxi soviet, executed by the Kuomintang; Xiang Jingyu (1895–1928), the Party’s first woman Central Committee member, executed in Wuhan; and Jiang Zhuyun (1920–1949), “Sister Jiang,” tortured and killed in Chongqing on the eve of liberation and later mythologized in the novel Red Crag.

ch01.anchor: the Flower World and the Great World
ch01.note: These six are Shanghai pleasure-houses. The first three — “Tower Beyond the Tower,” “Sky Beyond the Sky,” “Cloud Beyond the Cloud” — are old-style teahouse-and-restaurant towers; the New World (Xin Shijie, 1915) and above all the Great World (Da Shijie, 1917) were the vast multi-storey amusement arcades of Republican Shanghai, with stages, cinemas, food-stalls, games, and sideshows under one roof — the Great World the most famous popular entertainment palace in the city. The “Flower World” was a lesser house of the same kind.

ch01.anchor: grand Festival of the Hundred Entertainments
ch01.note: The “Hundred Entertainments” (baixi) were the variety spectacles of the Han court — acrobatics, music, animal acts and illusions under one bill; the “Fish and Dragon,” named just after, was a famous costume-transformation piece in which performers changed shape as a fish into a dragon.

ch01.anchor: the "Method of the Seven Sages"
ch01.note: Feats of the classical Chinese conjuring tradition: the “Dance into the Jar,” a Tang illusion of a body passing through vessels, and the “Method of the Seven Sages,” a decapitation-and-revival trick recorded in Tang tales. This home-grown sleight of hand, distinct from the imported Western stage magic that came later, is what the chapter means by “conjuring.”

ch01.anchor: "performed on a regular bill at the roof-garden theater of the Sincere Company"
ch01.note: The Sincere Company (Xianshi), opened on Nanjing Road in 1917, was one of the four great modern Chinese department stores of Shanghai; its upper floors held a roof garden with a theater and amusements.

ch01.anchor: The advertisement in the *Shen Bao* of November 9, 1930
ch01.note: The Shen Bao (“Shanghai News”), founded 1872, was the most important and longest-running newspaper of modern China and a chief record of Shanghai life until 1949.

ch01.anchor: to "the Green Gang hoodlum Yang Anqing,"
ch01.note: The Green Gang (Qingbang) was the dominant secret society and criminal brotherhood of Shanghai, with a grip on the docks, opium, gambling, and much of the labor market; its bosses, Du Yuesheng foremost, were powers in the city. Communist intelligence both fought the gang and used its members.

ch01.anchor: the former commander-in-chief of the Shanghai Workers' Pickets
ch01.note: In the Shanghai workers’ three armed uprisings of 1926–27, timed to the Northern Expedition’s approach, Communist-led pickets fought to seize the Chinese city from its warlord garrison; Gu Shunzhang commanded them in the third and successful rising of March 1927. Weeks later Chiang Kai-shek’s coup destroyed that short-lived workers’ government (see Section 4).

ch01.anchor: in 1922 I joined the S.Y. (the Socialist Youth League)
ch01.note: The Socialist Youth League (from 1925 the Communist Youth League) was the Party’s youth organization, founded 1920–22; many of the early Communists came up through it.

ch01.anchor: Gu Shunzhang's *Theory and Practice of Secret-Service Work* (1933) reproduces a chart
ch01.note: After his 1931 defection Gu Shunzhang wrote this manual of clandestine method for his new Nationalist masters; it is a chief source — hostile but expert — on the very service he had led.

ch01.anchor: the early-warning work on the International Settlement police side
ch01.note: Shanghai was divided among three jurisdictions: the International Settlement (British- and American-dominated), the French Concession, and the Chinese-governed city. The foreign concessions, each with its own police (the “patrol houses”) and courts and its limits on Chinese warrant service, were both the hunting ground and the refuge of the underground — which is why so much of this book turns on which force held which street.

ch01.anchor: he had schemed for Yuan Shikai and beaten the drum for monarchy
ch01.note: Yuan Shikai (1859–1916), the strongman general who forced the last Qing abdication, became the Republic’s first president and then, in 1915–16, tried to make himself emperor under the reign-title Hongxian; the attempt collapsed against nationwide revolt and he died months later. Yang Du was among the theorists who urged him on.

ch01.anchor: he founded the Baoding branch of the Tongmenghui
ch01.note: The Tongmenghui (“Revolutionary Alliance”), founded by Sun Yat-sen in Tokyo in 1905, was the chief organization of the anti-Qing revolution and the forerunner of the Kuomintang.

ch01.anchor: on the gallows of the warlord Zhang Zuolin
ch01.note: Zhang Zuolin (1875–1928), the “Old Marshal” of Manchuria, controlled Beijing in 1926–28; he had Li Dazhao and others hanged in April 1927 and was himself assassinated by the Japanese a year later.

ch01.anchor: "the three thousand retainers at the gate of Lord Chunshen"
ch01.note: Lord Chunshen was one of the “Four Lords” of the Warring States, famed for keeping three thousand retainers; his fief lay around the site of later Shanghai, whose short name, Shen, derives from him. To liken Du Yuesheng to him casts the gangster as a grand patron of talent.

ch01.anchor: the National Revolutionary Army swore its oath and marched north
ch01.note: The Northern Expedition (1926–28) was the great campaign, launched from Guangdong under the Kuomintang–Communist alliance, that broke the major warlords and nominally reunified China under the Nanjing government — in the course of which Chiang Kai-shek turned on his Communist allies.

ch01.anchor: now in a long gown and riding jacket, like the manager of a native bank
ch01.note: A “native bank” (qianzhuang) was a traditional Chinese money-house, distinct from the modern foreign-style banks; a “comprador” (maiban, named just above) was the Chinese manager who brokered a Western firm’s China business. Both were stock types of the Shanghai commercial world Chen Geng impersonated.

ch01.anchor: living in a *tingzijian*
ch01.note: A tingzijian was the small, dark room over the kitchen stairs of a Shanghai lane house, the cheapest lodging in the building; it became a byword for the hand-to-mouth life of the city’s writers and radicals.

ch01.anchor: looking very much like a Shanghai young master
ch01.note: “Young master” (xiaokai) is Shanghai slang for the idle, well-dressed son of a rich merchant house — a useful disguise for a man who had to seem to have money and no politics.

ch01.anchor: commander of the 386th Brigade of the 129th Division of the Eighteenth Group Army
ch01.note: The Eighteenth Group Army was the formal Nationalist designation, after the 1937 united front, of the Communist Eighth Route Army. Chen Geng’s 386th Brigade was so effective against the Japanese in the Shanxi mountains that captured enemy vehicles were found painted “Kill the 386th Brigade.”

ch01.anchor: overcome subjectivism in our operations through the Rectification
ch01.note: The Rectification Movement (zhengfeng) was the Party-wide campaign of study and self-criticism launched at the Yan’an base in 1942 to unify doctrine and discipline; “mopping-up” (saodang) was the Japanese army’s term for its sweeps against the Communist guerrilla areas.

ch01.anchor: as Bo Yibo, who fought at his side in those days
ch01.note: Bo Yibo (1908–2007) was a senior Communist leader in north China, later a vice-premier and one of the Party’s “eight elders” of the reform era.

ch01.anchor: Xu Kexiang and Xia Douyin
ch01.note: The purge’s enforcers. Yang Hu and Chen Qun ran the “party purification” terror in Shanghai; He Jian, the Hunan commander, executed thousands (among them Mao Zedong’s wife, Yang Kaihui); Xu Kexiang led the bloody Changsha coup of May 21, 1927; Xia Douyin revolted against the Wuhan government. “Better to kill a thousand by mistake than let one slip the net” became the byword of the White Terror.

ch01.anchor: By the Party's own partial count at its Sixth Congress
ch01.note: The Chinese Communist Party’s Sixth National Congress met in secret near Moscow in mid-1928 — the only one of its congresses held on foreign soil — to take stock after the catastrophe of 1927.

ch01.anchor: glimpsed in Li Yimang's late recollections
ch01.note: Li Yimang (1903–1990) was a Communist writer, diplomat, and cultural official whose memoirs are a much-used source for the early underground.

ch01.anchor: Ren Bishi, Gu Shunzhang, Luo Yinong, Xiang Zhongfa, Zhou Enlai, Zhang Tailei, Li Lisan, Deng Zhongxia, Cai Hesen, Ren Xu and others took part
ch01.note: A roll of the Party’s 1927 leadership. Xiang Zhongfa (1880–1931), a dockworker raised up as nominal General Secretary, was captured and shot in 1931 (his end is the subject of a later chapter). Zhang Tailei was killed leading the Canton Uprising weeks after this meeting; Luo Yinong, Cai Hesen, and Deng Zhongxia were all executed by the Nationalists (1928, 1931, 1933); Li Lisan gave his name to the ultra-left “Li Lisan line” of 1930; Ren Bishi rose to the Party’s inner core by 1949.

ch01.anchor: a Shanghai-style shikumen lane house of three upper rooms
ch01.note: The shikumen (“stone-framed gate”) row house — a two- or three-storey brick terrace opening onto a narrow lane (longtang) — was the characteristic domestic architecture of modern Shanghai and, with its warren of rooms and back stairs, the natural habitat of the underground.

ch01.anchor: The Fifth National Congress of the Chinese Communist Party had just closed.
ch01.note: The Party’s Fifth Congress met at Wuhan in April–May 1927, even as Chiang Kai-shek’s Shanghai coup was breaking the united front.

ch01.anchor: making its name across the three towns of Wuhan
ch01.note: “The three towns of Wuhan” are Wuchang, Hankou, and Hanyang, the tri-city on the middle Yangtze that was the seat of the Nationalist left government in 1927.

ch01.anchor: a former parliament member of the Beiyang era
ch01.note: The “Beiyang” period (1912–28) is the era of the warlord-dominated Republican government in Beijing, named for the Beiyang Army from which its strongmen sprang.

ch01.anchor: together with Guo Moruo, Yang Hansheng, and Li Yimang
ch01.note: Guo Moruo (1892–1978), poet, playwright, and historian, became the towering literary official of the People’s Republic; Yang Hansheng (1902–1993) was a leading left-wing dramatist and screenwriter. Both, like Mei Gongbin, joined the Nanchang Uprising.

ch01.anchor: the peasant uprising under Peng Pai
ch01.note: Peng Pai (1896–1929), the “king of the peasant movement,” built China’s first rural soviet at Hailufeng in Guangdong; he was captured and executed in Shanghai in 1929.

ch01.anchor: came to know Chen Mingshu and Li Jishen
ch01.note: Chen Mingshu (1889–1965) and Li Jishen (1885–1959) were senior Cantonese generals of the Nineteenth Route Army who broke with Chiang Kai-shek; both later helped found the Revolutionary Committee of the Kuomintang and served the People’s Republic.

ch01.anchor: In the "January Twenty-Eighth" Shanghai War
ch01.note: On January 28, 1932 the Japanese attacked Shanghai; the Nineteenth Route Army’s month-long resistance, against Nanjing’s wishes, made it a national hero and set the stage for its later revolt.

ch01.anchor: held closely together around the Party's Central Southern Bureau under Zhou Enlai
ch01.note: The Southern Bureau, led by Zhou Enlai from wartime Chongqing, directed Communist united-front work in Nationalist-held China.

ch01.anchor: a delegate to the first plenary session of the CPPCC
ch01.note: The Chinese People’s Political Consultative Conference (CPPCC) and the National People’s Congress (NPC) are, respectively, China’s advisory assembly of parties and notables and its legislature; seats in them were the public honors by which a hidden Communist like Mei Gongbin lived out his cover.

ch01.anchor: the Naigai Cotton Company's No. 7 Mill
ch01.note: The Naigai Cotton Company (Naigai Wata) was a large Japanese-owned textile firm whose Shanghai mills, working Chinese labor under harsh conditions, were a focus of the 1925 unrest.

ch01.anchor: A worker of the mill, Gu Zhenghong
ch01.note: Gu Zhenghong (1905–1925), a Communist worker-organizer shot by a Japanese overseer on May 15, 1925, was the martyr whose death touched off the May Thirtieth Movement two weeks later.

ch01.anchor: He attended the Party's Third Congress in 1923
ch01.note: The Party’s Third Congress (Guangzhou, 1923) resolved on the first united front with the Kuomintang — the policy whose collapse in 1927 gives this book its subject.

ch01.anchor: deciding how the Party would operate in the White areas
ch01.note: “White areas” (baiqu) meant the territory under Nationalist control, as against the Communist-held “red” or “Soviet areas” (suqu); clandestine work in the White areas is the whole theater of this book.

ch01.anchor: the Red Army in the Soviet areas, and the Communist International.
ch01.note: The Communist International (Comintern), the Moscow-led federation of the world’s Communist parties (1919–43), directed and funded the Chinese party in this period and trained its cadres; its policy lines and its money run through the whole story.

ch01.anchor: men of "give me liberty or give me death,"
ch01.note: The phrase renders the Chinese bu ziyou, wu ning si, itself an echo of Patrick Henry’s revolutionary cry of 1775; the author reaches for a Western touchstone of the free conscience.

ch01.anchor: the War of Resistance against Japan
ch01.note: The War of Resistance against Japan (1937–1945), China’s war against the Japanese invasion and the Chinese theater of the Second World War; its “final victory” came with Japan’s surrender in August 1945.

ch02.anchor: Zong Mengping was one of them; Kuang Yaming was another
ch02.note: Zong Mengping (1907–?) and Kuang Yaming (1906–1996) were Communist organizers in the Yixing area of southern Jiangsu. Zong is an obscure figure whose intelligence work is known chiefly from the Party’s own recollections (such as the memoir the author quotes below) and is not corroborated in the wider scholarship. Kuang Yaming became far better known after 1949 as an educator and long-serving president of Nanjing University.

ch02.anchor: an emergency conference in Hankou
ch02.note: The August 7 Conference (Baqi huiyi) of 1927, held in secret at Hankou after the collapse of the Communist–Kuomintang alliance. It ended Chen Duxiu’s leadership, installed Qu Qiubai, and set the Party on a new course of armed uprising and agrarian revolution. It was here that Mao Zedong made his often-quoted remark that “political power grows out of the barrel of a gun.” Hankou is one of the three towns that make up Wuhan.

ch02.anchor: an Autumn Harvest Uprising as the Party's foremost task
ch02.note: A wave of Communist-led peasant risings in the autumn of 1927, timed to the harvest, following the August 7 Conference’s call to arms. The best known was the Autumn Harvest Uprising in the Hunan–Jiangxi border country led by Mao Zedong that September; its survivors regrouped at the Jinggang Mountains and became the nucleus of the Red Army.

ch02.anchor: the heads of the Jiangnan counties together in Shanghai
ch02.note: Jiangnan, literally “south of the river,” is the rich, densely settled region just south of the lower Yangtze — here the counties around Shanghai and Lake Tai, including Yixing, Wuxi, and Jiangyin.

ch02.anchor: the Shrine of Chastity and Filial Piety in Yicheng
ch02.note: A jiexiao ci, a hall erected by the imperial state to honor chaste widows who never remarried and exemplary filial sons. Such shrines stood in most county seats; a revolutionary cell meeting in one is a small irony the author lets pass without comment. Yicheng was the seat of Yixing county.

ch02.anchor: and Shi Yanfen as his deputies
ch02.note: Shi Yanfen (1904–1928), a Yixing native and one of the leaders of the local rising, is not to be confused with Shi Yaobin, the county committee secretary named earlier. Arrested in Nanjing in May 1928, he refused under four months of interrogation to give anything away and was executed at Yuhuatai on September 27, 1928, aged twenty-five. The blood-stained farewell letter to his younger brother and sister, found in his clothing, is among the best known of the Communist prison testaments.

ch02.anchor: posted him to Rugao to head the Relief Society there
ch02.note: The Relief Society (Jinanhui), the Chinese section of International Red Aid (MOPR), the Comintern’s body for supporting jailed and persecuted revolutionaries and their families. Under Kuomintang repression it operated as a semi-clandestine Communist front.

ch02.anchor: with Chen Yun and others, formed a farmers' commission
ch02.note: Chen Yun (1905–1995), then a young labor and peasant organizer in Jiangsu, rose to the Party’s Politburo Standing Committee and, after 1949, became the chief architect of the People’s Republic’s economy and one of its most powerful elder statesmen. His involvement in the Central Special Branch, described later in this passage, is a lesser-known chapter of his early career.

ch02.anchor: pressing a campaign of surrenders
ch02.note: The Kuomintang’s zishou (“surrender” or “self-repentance”) policy: captured or wavering Communists were pressed to publish notices in the newspapers renouncing the Party and pledging loyalty to the government. A published recantation was the standard proof of a break with the Party — which is exactly why it made such effective cover for an agent being planted inside enemy lines.

ch02.anchor: faced them and said, with righteous force
ch02.note: Luo Qingchang (1918–2014), whom the citation credits, was a veteran of the Party’s intelligence service who rose to head the Central Investigation Department and was long regarded as the custodian of Zhou Enlai’s legacy in secret work; his recollections are a standard Party source for this history.

ch02.anchor: Wronged and unbowed in heart
ch02.note: A classical maxim in the spirit of the Confucian Analects: only under pressure and injustice is the true gentleman (junzi) revealed. The author uses it to close the account of Kuang Yaming’s refusal to break.

ch02.anchor: riches could not corrupt, poverty could not sway, and force could not bend
ch02.note: The three marks of the “great man” (da zhangfu) from the Mencius (3B.2): “Riches and honor cannot corrupt him, poverty and low station cannot sway him, power and force cannot bend him.” It is one of the most quoted passages in the Confucian canon.

ch02.anchor: overwhelm every enemy and never be subdued by any
ch02.note: From Mao Zedong’s report “On Coalition Government,” delivered to the Party’s Seventh Congress in April 1945, where he wrote that the people’s army “has an indomitable spirit and is determined to vanquish all enemies and never to yield.” The author borrows the line, written of the Red Army, and applies it to the fighters of the hidden front.

ch02.anchor: Chen Duxiu, Peng Shuzhi, Luo Yinong, Zhao Shiyan, and Wang Shouhua were all of a mind
ch02.note: The five leaders of the Party’s Shanghai apparatus in 1927. Chen Duxiu (1879–1942) was the Party’s co-founder and first general secretary, blamed after 1927 for its defeat and later expelled as a Trotskyist. Peng Shuzhi (1895–1983) followed him into the Trotskyist opposition. Luo Yinong (1902–1928), Zhao Shiyan (1901–1927), and Wang Shouhua (1899–1927), the field commanders of the three armed uprisings, were all seized and killed within a year — Wang Shouhua strangled by Du Yuesheng’s gangsters on the eve of the April 12 coup, Zhao and Luo executed soon after.

ch02.anchor: the Shanghai Provisional Municipal Government opened for business
ch02.note: Set up on March 22–23, 1927, the day after the third armed uprising of the Shanghai workers drove out the warlord garrison, this was the first municipal government founded by a popular revolt in a major Chinese city. Its nineteen-member committee mixed Communists (Luo Yinong, Wang Shouhua), Kuomintang men (Bai Chongxi, Niu Yongjian), and Shanghai businessmen. It lasted about three weeks; Chiang Kai-shek’s coup of April 12, 1927 swept it away.

ch02.anchor: Welcome the Northern Expedition Army to Shanghai
ch02.note: The Northern Expedition (1926–1928) was the military campaign by which the Kuomintang, then allied with the Communists, marched north from Guangdong to break the warlords and unify China. Its approach to Shanghai in the spring of 1927 was the signal for the workers’ uprisings; within weeks its commander, Chiang Kai-shek, turned on his Communist allies.

ch02.anchor: openly propagate the C.P.
ch02.note: “C.P.” — the Communist Party, from the English initials, used as shorthand in the Party’s own documents of the period. The abbreviation is reproduced as it stands in the quoted resolution.

ch02.anchor: the Shanghai General Labor Union counted 502 affiliated unions and 820,000 members
ch02.note: The Shanghai General Labor Union (Shanghai zong gonghui), the Communist-led federation of the city’s trade unions, was the organizing force behind the three workers’ uprisings of 1926–27 and, at its height, claimed to speak for the great majority of the city’s industrial workforce.

ch02.anchor: a textbook lumpen proletarian
ch02.note: “Lumpen proletariat” (German Lumpenproletariat, rendered in Chinese as liumang wuchanzhe, literally “hoodlum propertyless”) is Marx’s term for the drifting underclass beneath the working class — the vagrants, criminals, and casual toughs he judged unreliable for revolution and easily bought by reaction. The section title turns the label on Gu Shunzhang, and the chapter’s argument is that his gangster instincts, not his politics, are the key to his eventual treason.

ch02.anchor: the marvelous portrait Mao Zedong once drew of men of his kind
ch02.note: From Mao Zedong’s “Analysis of the Classes in Chinese Society” (1925), the essay that opens his Selected Works. Mao classed the “lumpen proletariat” — the uprooted men of the secret societies — as brave but destructive, and salvageable for revolution only under firm guidance. The author quotes it to explain both why Zhou Enlai thought Gu Shunzhang usable and why he proved a danger.

ch02.anchor: the Triads in Fujian and Guangdong
ch02.note: The secret societies Mao lists were sworn brotherhoods of the poor and uprooted, part mutual-aid lodge and part criminal fraternity: the Triads (Sanhehui) of the south coast; the Elder Brothers Society (Gelaohui) of the Yangtze provinces; the Big Sword Society (Dadaohui) of the north China plain; the Society of the Way (Zailihui) of the northeast; and the Green Gang (Qingbang) of Shanghai, the most powerful of all, whose boss Du Yuesheng supplied the muscle for Chiang Kai-shek’s 1927 purge. “Zhili” was the old name for the province around Beijing; “the three eastern provinces” means Manchuria.

ch02.anchor: a foreman at the cigarette works of the Nanyang Brothers Tobacco Company as well
ch02.note: The Nanyang Brothers Tobacco Company, founded in 1905, was the great Chinese-owned rival to the British-American Tobacco combine and one of the largest native industrial firms in Shanghai. A shop foreman there stood over the workers and hired and fired at the gate — a natural perch for a man who ran gangs on the side.

ch02.anchor: (John Byron and Robert Pack, 1998)
ch02.note: John Byron and Robert Pack, The Claws of the Dragon: Kang Sheng — the Evil Genius Behind Mao (1992; Chinese translation 1998), a Western biography of the Party’s later intelligence chief that also treats the early history of its secret service.

ch02.anchor: (Cai Mengjian, 1980)
ch02.note: Cai Mengjian (1905–2001) was the Kuomintang intelligence officer in Wuhan who arrested Gu Shunzhang in April 1931 and wired the news to Nanjing — the message intercepted by the Communist mole Qian Zhuangfei, the warning that let the Shanghai underground escape. His memoirs are a Nationalist-side source on Gu.

ch02.anchor: director of the Central Women's Commission, and head of the women workers' department of the All-China Federation of Labor
ch02.note: Yang Zhihua (1901–1973), a leading woman organizer of the Party and the wife of its onetime chief Qu Qiubai. “Du Ning,” the name under which the passage is cited, was one of her pen names; the reader should not take it for a separate authority.

ch02.anchor: open formal talks with Xue Yue
ch02.note: Xue Yue (1896–1998), then a division commander in the Northern Expedition forces at Shanghai and briefly sympathetic to the Left, later became one of the Nationalists’ ablest field generals, famous for the defense of Changsha against the Japanese. The plan here was to draft the unreliable pickets into his ranks and so be rid of them.

ch02.anchor: like the Green Gang opening its initiation hall
ch02.note: “Opening the incense hall” (kai xiangtang) was the Green Gang’s formal initiation rite, at which recruits knelt before the altar, swore the brotherhood’s oaths, and bound themselves to a master. The author’s point is that Gu Shunzhang recruited for the Party as a gang boss recruits for his gang.

ch02.anchor: a word with a spine in it
ch02.note: The chapter is titled with a common Chinese saying, qing zhe zi qing, zhuo zhe zi zhuo — literally “the clear stays clear of itself, the muddy stays muddy of itself.” The sense is that the honest need no defending and the corrupt cannot be washed clean: character will out. It frames the chapter’s contrast between the incorruptible underground heroes of the first section and the gangster Gu Shunzhang of the second.

ch03.anchor: no confidence-man
ch03.note: A chaibaidang: one of the swindlers of old Shanghai who courted a woman under false pretenses to strip her of her money. The list here runs from the petty street ruffian up to this practiced confidence-man.

ch03.anchor: 178 Rue Bourgeat in the Shanghai French Concession
ch03.note: Like the other streets of the French Concession, this one bore a French name; it is Changle Road today. Throughout the chapter the author gives such present-day names in parentheses, a help to the modern Shanghai reader.

ch03.anchor: a comprador for a motorcar company
ch03.note: A comprador (maiban) was the Chinese manager who handled a foreign firm's dealings with the local market. The title carried an air of wealth and Western connection, which is why the caller offers it as a credential.

ch03.anchor: member of the Standing Committee of the Party's Central Politburo
ch03.note: Luo Yinong (1902–1928) rose through the Shanghai workers' movement to the Party's top councils. His arrest and execution in April 1928, the subject of this chapter, are recorded across the Party's own accounts; the shooting at Longhua is usually dated April 21, 1928.

ch03.anchor: Communist University of the Toilers of the East in Moscow
ch03.note: Known by its Russian initials KUTV, this Comintern school in Moscow trained revolutionaries from across Asia; a great part of the early Chinese Communist leadership passed through it.

ch03.anchor: speaking at a forum marking the hundredth anniversary of Luo Yinong's birth
ch03.note: Hu Jintao was then General Secretary of the Communist Party and, from 2003, President of China (in office to 2012–13). Such centenary tributes are the Party's formal way of fixing a figure's place in its own history.

ch03.anchor: though Zheng Chaolin says number 123
ch03.note: Zheng Chaolin (1901–1998), editor of Bolshevik and later a leading Chinese Trotskyist, spent decades in Nationalist and then Communist prisons. His detailed memoirs are among the fullest first-hand sources for the underground of these years, and the author leans on them heavily, discrepancies and all.

ch03.anchor: Xiang embroidery from Changsha
ch03.note: Xiang xiu, the silk embroidery of Hunan, is counted one of China's four great embroidery traditions; Changsha is its center. That so much of it hung on the walls is the author's quiet mark of a household living beyond an underground worker's means.

ch03.anchor: the large pearls and the small came pattering onto the jade plate
ch03.note: An echo of Bai Juyi's Song of the Pipa (9th century), whose famous line likens the notes of the lute to large and small pearls falling on a plate of jade. Li Zheshi is remembering how easily Qu Qiubai, unlike her husband, could make music.

ch03.anchor: you cut it and it will not part, you smooth it and it snarls again
ch03.note: From a lyric by Li Yu (937–978), the last ruler of the Southern Tang, on the tangle of parting sorrow; the next phrase Li Zheshi quotes, “a taste all its own upon the heart,” is from the same poem.

ch03.anchor: Lu Xun's Wandering
ch03.note: Panghuang (1926), the second collection of short stories by Lu Xun (1881–1936), modern China's foremost writer. The Beixin Book Company was a well-known Shanghai literary press.

ch03.anchor: the White Terror was severe
ch03.note: The wave of arrests and executions the Kuomintang loosed on the Communists from April 1927, which drove the Party underground and forms the backdrop to this whole book.

ch03.anchor: said that Chen Yannian
ch03.note: Chen Yannian (1898–1927), eldest son of the Party's founder Chen Duxiu and secretary of its Jiangsu committee, was captured and killed in Shanghai in the summer of 1927. His younger brother Chen Qiaonian, named earlier at the wedding, was killed the following year.

ch03.anchor: Xia Minghan, and others were killed one after another
ch03.note: Xia Minghan (1900–1928), a Hunan Communist, was executed at Wuhan in March 1928, leaving the much-quoted lines “kill me, no matter—there are those who come after.” The source prints his given name with a variant character (the martyr's name is standardly written 夏明翰).

ch03.anchor: the editorial office of Bolshevik and Zheng Chaolin's home
ch03.note: Bolshevik (Bu'ersaiweike) was the Party Center's chief theoretical journal from 1927 to 1932, edited in this very house.

ch03.anchor: east of Hardoon Garden
ch03.note: The vast walled estate (Aili Garden) of Silas Aaron Hardoon, a Baghdadi-Jewish magnate who became one of Shanghai's richest men; it was a landmark of the western Settlement.

ch03.anchor: a hotel near the Great World
ch03.note: The Great World (Da Shijie), a many-storied amusement arcade opened in 1917, was among the most famous pleasure resorts of Shanghai and a useful crowd to disappear into.

ch03.anchor: Later still came Deng Xiaoping
ch03.note: Deng Xiaoping (1904–1997), then a young secretary at the Party Center and here an eyewitness to Luo Yinong's arrest, would half a century later become China's paramount leader. His daughter's memoir, cited below as Maomao, is the source for his account.

ch03.anchor: men of the Green and Red Gangs
ch03.note: The two great Shanghai secret societies. The Green Gang (see the note at Chapter Two) controlled the concession underworld; both were courted, and feared, by every side. Working through them to reach the authorities was standard practice.

ch03.anchor: from the concession to Longhua
ch03.note: Longhua, on Shanghai's southern edge, held the headquarters of the Songhu (Shanghai–Woosung) Garrison and its execution ground, where many Communists were shot in these years. A Chinese prisoner handed over from the foreign concession would be taken there.

ch03.anchor: Qian Dajun, Commander of the Songhu Garrison
ch03.note: Qian Dajun (1893–1982), a senior Kuomintang general close to Chiang Kai-shek, commanded the Shanghai garrison that carried out the execution.

ch03.anchor: By order of Chiang ××
ch03.note: The two crosses stand in the source itself, which reproduces the notice with the words after Chiang's name struck out; nothing has been supplied here.

ch03.anchor: the concubine Comrade Zhu De took
ch03.note: Zhu De (1886–1976), a former Yunnan officer who joined the Party in Germany in 1922 and later became commander-in-chief of the Red Army and the PLA. That He Zhihua was his wife (the scholarship writes her name He Zhihua, 贺治华) and bore him a daughter is well attested; it is the fact that turns this chapter's traitor into a figure out of the Party's own founding household.

ch03.anchor: a daughter by Zhu De, Zhu Min
ch03.note: Zhu Min (1926–2009), Zhu De's only surviving child, was raised apart from both parents and reared largely by her grandmother; her memoir is the source for the family scenes quoted here.

ch03.anchor: one of Zhang Zuolin's spies
ch03.note: Zhang Zuolin (1875–1928), the Fengtian warlord who then controlled Beijing and hunted Communists ferociously; to be taken for his agent was a grave suspicion.

ch03.anchor: on Bubbling Well Road
ch03.note: A principal road of the International Settlement running west past Jing'an (“Bubbling Well”) Temple; it is Nanjing West Road today.

ch03.anchor: under Kang Sheng
ch03.note: One of the conflicting later accounts puts a young Kang Sheng (1898–1975) at the head of the killing party. Kang, then a Shanghai underground cadre, would rise to run the Party's security apparatus and become one of the most feared figures of the Cultural Revolution; the attribution is uncorroborated and the author reports it only as one version.

ch03.anchor: The Road Through Vicissitudes
ch03.note: A popular 2009 Chinese television drama (Renjian Zhengdao Shi Cangsang) whose fictional hero Liqing is loosely modeled on figures of the underground war. The author cites it to show how the episode has passed into legend, not as evidence.

ch03.anchor: the concession's Mixed Court
ch03.note: The Huishen Gongxie, the tribunal of mixed foreign and Chinese jurisdiction that handled cases arising in the concessions.

ch03.anchor: the Abbé Faria says
ch03.note: The learned old prisoner of Alexandre Dumas's The Count of Monte Cristo, who teaches the hero to find a crime's author by asking who profits from it—the ancient maxim cui bono. The author borrows it to reopen the question of He Zhihua's motive.

ch03.anchor: recruited Yang Dengying (also called Bao Junfu)
ch03.note: Yang Dengying, under the cover name Bao Junfu, became the Party's first double agent planted inside the enemy's own intelligence service—the coup that opens the next chapter.

ch03.anchor: The "Zhihua" of Zhu De's letter is He Zhihua
ch03.note: The narration writes her name He Zhihua with the character 稚; Zhu De's letter, and most of the scholarship, write it with 治. The two are homophones (both romanize Zhihua) and denote the same woman; the discrepancy is the source's, left as printed.

ch03.anchor: shot her in the courtyard
ch03.note: That He Zhihua survived the 1928 attack, fled, and was later killed is agreed; the manner and date are not. The book places her death at Kaijiang in 1938; other accounts give different years and circumstances. The disagreement is noted here and left unresolved, as the author himself leaves it.

ch03.anchor: gather the moon nearest the water
ch03.note: From the couplet “the pavilion by the water gets the moon first” (jinshui loutai xian de yue): whoever is best placed reaps the advantage first. He Zhihua, placed close to Luo Yinong by her work, means to seize the opening.

ch04.note: The chapter opens with the writer Lu Xun (1881–1936), the towering figure of modern Chinese literature, on how censors' cuts were marked in print. The works he names are the notoriously erotic Ming novel Jin Ping Mei (rendered here Plum in the Golden Vase) and the two Ming vernacular story collections Chuke Pai'an Jingqi and Erke Pai'an Jingqi (Slapping the Table in Amazement, first and second); the ancient Mu Tianzi Zhuan (Tale of King Mu, Son of Heaven) is his example of a genuine textual lacuna. Expurgated editions replaced the cut passages with little empty squares.

“Opening a skylight” (kai tianchuang) is the Chinese printers' term for leaving a censored space visibly blank on the page, so that readers see exactly where something was struck out. Lu Xun's point is that Chinese-language papers were forced to run such blanks (or the marks “□□” and “××”) where a passage was killed, whereas the foreign-language press, beyond the reach of the same censors, could print the story in full.

The North China Daily News (Chinese Zilin Xibao) was the leading English-language newspaper of Shanghai, published 1864–1951 and widely regarded as the voice of the British business community; being foreign-run, it lay outside the Chinese censorship that silenced the local Chinese papers.

ch04.anchor: Peng Pai was then a member of the CCP Central Politburo
ch04.note: Peng Pai (1896–1929), from Haifeng in Guangdong, was the Party's foremost organizer of peasants—“the king of the peasant movement”—and founder of the Hailufeng Soviet of 1927–28, the first rural soviet in China. His arrest and execution here are the central event of the chapter. Corroborated across the Party-history literature.

Yang Yin (1892–1929), from Zhongshan in Guangdong, was a leader of the December 1927 Guangzhou Uprising and head of the CCP's Central Military Department; he was arrested with Peng Pai and shot with him at Longhua on August 30, 1929.

Yan Changyi (1898–1929) and Xing Shizhen were the two other Communists executed with Peng Pai and Yang Yin—the four commemorated together in Party memory as “Peng, Yang, Yan, and Xing.” Yan had been slated to take over Peng Pai's military work; Xing ran the Party's work among enemy soldiers in Jiangsu.

Bai Xin (1903–1929), a Hunanese, was secretary of the CCP Central Military Commission when he secretly surrendered to the Kuomintang and betrayed the August 24, 1929 meeting, sending Peng Pai and the others to their deaths. The Special Branch killed him on Avenue Joffre on November 11, 1929, in a case the Shanghai press called “the East's greatest assassination.” His treachery is corroborated by the Party's own contemporary accounts and by later scholarship.

Chen Lifu (1900–2001) and his elder brother Chen Guofu (1892–1951) headed the “CC Clique,” the Kuomintang faction that ran the party apparatus and its civilian intelligence. The Investigation Section of the Central Organization Department, set up here, grew into the service later known as the Zhongtong (the Central Bureau of Investigation and Statistics). Zhang Daofan (1897–1968) was a CC-Clique official and propagandist.

ch04.anchor: It was a café kept by White Russians
ch04.note: After the Bolshevik victory tens of thousands of White Russians—monarchists and others who had fled the Revolution and Civil War—settled in Shanghai, many of them destitute former aristocrats. Their cafés, restaurants, and nightclubs, clustered in the French Concession, were a distinctive feature of the city between the wars.

Duško Popov (1912–1981) was a Yugoslav lawyer who served in the Second World War as a British double agent, codenamed “Tricycle” (he ran a ring of three), feeding the German Abwehr disinformation vetted by MI5 while reporting to British intelligence; he contributed to the Normandy deception and is widely cited as an inspiration for Ian Fleming's James Bond. The comparison is the author's own; the details of Popov's career are corroborated (Wikipedia; UK National Archives).

An E (1905–1976), born Zhang Shiyuan, was a poet and lyricist whom the Party planted as Yang Dengying's secretary, handled on a single line by Chen Geng. She later wrote the words of “The Newsboy's Song” (with the composer Nie Er) and married the playwright Tian Han, author of the lyrics of China's national anthem. Corroborated (Chinese Wikipedia; Baidu Baike).

Sun Yat-sen University in Moscow (1925–1930) was a Comintern school founded to train Chinese revolutionaries of both the Communist and the Nationalist parties; it is distinct from the University of the Toilers of the East (KUTV), the older Comintern school mentioned elsewhere in this book.

ch04.anchor: Ke Lin, a physician of the first rank
ch04.note: Ke Lin (1901–1991), from Haifeng in Guangdong, was a Communist physician who ran the Dasheng Hospital in Shanghai as a Party front (with He Cheng, alias He Yusheng) and served the Special Branch; after 1935 he spent decades in Macau, for many years director of the Kiang Wu Hospital. Corroborated (Chinese academic and official sources).

The Guangzhou (Canton) Uprising of December 11–13, 1927, in which Communists briefly held the city and proclaimed a “Canton Commune,” was the last of the Party's failed 1927 urban risings; it was crushed within days with heavy loss of life.

ch04.anchor: the Shanghai Republican Daily carried two reports at once
ch04.note: The Republican Daily (Minguo Ribao) was the Kuomintang's Shanghai organ; the notice it planted here—that Bai Xin had merely been “duped” into the Party and bailed out by Chiang Kai-shek—was cover to disguise the fact that he had become the Nationalists' agent.

“The Internationale,” the international anthem of the socialist and communist movement, was the customary song of Chinese Communists facing execution; here Peng Pai and his comrades sing it on their way to the firing squad.

Dong Jianwu (1891–1970), introduced in Chapter One, was the “Red Pastor”: a graduate of St. John's University (and a schoolfellow of T. V. Soong) who joined the Party after 1927 and used his church as cover for Special Branch liaison work under Chen Geng. He is best remembered for later sheltering Mao Zedong's sons and arranging, with Zhang Xueliang's help, to send two of them to the Soviet Union.

ch04.anchor: St. Peter's Church on Avenue Road
ch04.note: St. Peter's Church, an Anglican church on Avenue Road consecrated in 1898, is not to be confused with the Baptist Grace Church (Huai'en Tang) on Seymour Road, completed only in 1942; the author corrects a source that conflates the two.

Avenue Joffre, the grand tree-lined boulevard at the heart of the French Concession (today Huaihai Middle Road), was named for the French Marshal Joseph Joffre; the chapter title, “Bloodshed on Avenue Joffre,” refers to the killing of Bai Xin in a lane off it.

Huang Jinrong (1868–1953) was the pre-eminent boss of the Green Gang and, at the same time, a detective in the French Concession police—the archetype of the gangster-official of old Shanghai. His house was used to hide the wounded Fan Zhengbo.

Luo Qingchang (1918–2014) was a veteran of the Party's intelligence services who rose to head the Central Investigation Department and to direct work on Taiwan; he was the last department head Zhou Enlai received, days before the Premier lost the power of speech.

ch04.anchor: Qincheng Prison to question Bao Junfu
ch04.note: Qincheng, near Beijing, is China's high-security political prison. The author's argument is that placing Yang Dengying there during the Cultural Revolution was, paradoxically, Zhou Enlai's only means of protecting a former double agent from the Red Guards—a shelter disguised as detention.

Zhang Jichun, deputy commander of the Shanghai General Labor Union pickets, was the fifth man seized at Jingyuanli; unlike Peng Pai, Yang Yin, Yan Changyi, and Xing Shizhen, he was not among the four executed on August 30, 1929.

The sources the author quotes disagree on the house number: most give No. 12 Jingyuanli, but this one gives No. 1015. Both are reproduced here as printed; the discrepancy is the source's, not the translation's.

ch05.note: “Sima Road” means “Fourth Horse Road.” The east–west streets of the International Settlement were known in Chinese by number as malu, “horse roads”: First (today Nanjing East Road), Second (Jiujiang Road), Third or Sanma Road (today Hankou Road), Fourth or Sima Road (today Fuzhou Road), Fifth (Guangdong Road). Fourth Horse Road was famous for its bookshops and teahouses, its theaters and its brothels alike.

Xiong Jinding (1886–1973), the “Red Boss,” managed the underground Party’s money in Shanghai from 1928 and, with Zhu Duanshou, kept the Yunnan Road safe house that doubled as the Politburo’s meeting place. He came through the underground years, held finance and united-front posts after 1949, and is the central figure of this chapter. Corroborated across the Party-history literature.

The Shanghai Race Club’s course (the paomating), a great grandstand and turf oval that the British ran in the heart of the settlement, at the west end of Fourth Horse Road; the grounds are today People’s Park and People’s Square.

ch05.anchor: a solid shop to stand surety
ch05.note: To rent property in Shanghai one commonly needed a pubao—a going concern of known standing willing to vouch for the tenant and answer for the rent. A stranger with no local ties could not readily produce one. This is the author’s point against the romantic “found it by chance in the rain” version: a safe house was hard to secure, and the finding of it was the First Section’s trade, not a lone accountant’s luck.

The betrayal recounted in Chapter Three: in 1928 He Jiaxing and his wife He Zhihua gave up Luo Yinong, a member of the Politburo Standing Committee, to the concession police, and he was shot. Here the author invokes it to show how wary landlords were of tenants who spoke the wrong dialect.

Nan Hanchen (1895–1967) was the first governor of the People’s Bank of China, founded in 1949, and later chairman of the China Council for the Promotion of International Trade; an old hand at the Party’s underground finance, which is why the Xiongs’ appeal came to his desk.

Xiong Xiaosan was a Nationalist general and Xiong Jinding’s son by an earlier marriage; father and son took opposite sides after 1927. Zhou Enlai’s statement records that he received his father’s letter urging him to come over during the Huaihai Campaign (1948–49) but held out, and fled when the Communists attacked.

From a couplet Xiong Jinding wrote in old age (the 1987 date is that of the source that prints it). “Fish and water” (yushui) is the stock Chinese figure for a perfect, inseparable union, of ruler and minister or of husband and wife; the line sums up his four decades and more with Zhu Duanshou.

Wuhao was Zhou Enlai’s best-known cover name in the underground years. It was later turned against him: in 1932 the Nationalists planted a forged notice, the so-called “Wuhao renouncing the Party” announcement, over his alias—a slander revived to attack him in the Cultural Revolution.

A wash of alum dissolved in water was a standard developer for invisible ink: a message written in a colorless solution and dried would come up again when brushed over with the alum wash. The Special Branch used it on documents sent up from the soviet areas.

Chao bazi, literally “going through the target,” was Shanghai slang for the concession police’s snap body-searches in the street or at a checkpoint—the standing hazard for a courier carrying documents on their person.

Zhibu Shenghuo, an internal bulletin of the Party’s central-organs branch, edited by Deng Yingchao, Zhou Enlai’s wife. A print run of seventy-five copies gives the measure of how small and closed the underground apparatus was.

A play on sound: the branch’s abbreviation (zhizhi, “directly subordinate”) and its codename (zhizhi, “plant a branch”) are homophones written with different characters—a small piece of underground wordcraft.

In the shikumen lanes, which had no plumbing, each household’s night-soil bucket (matong) was carried out at dawn to be emptied at the lane’s collection point and scrubbed in the street—women’s work by custom. The debate Zhu Duanshou relished turned a chamber pot into a question of the sexes’ equality; Zhou Enlai’s counter was that a household that broke the custom would catch a watcher’s eye.

Hongshao shizitou, “red-cooked lion’s heads”—oversized pork meatballs braised until meltingly soft, a signature of Huaiyang cooking from the lower Yangtze. The name likens the big meatball, ringed with cabbage, to a lion’s maned head; the dish gives the section its title.

ch05.anchor: Preface to the Pavilion of Prince Teng
ch05.note: Wang Bo (c. 650–676), a prodigy of the early Tang, wrote this celebrated rhapsody. The line Xiong Jinding read out—“The setting glow and a lone wild duck fly as one; the autumn waters and the boundless sky are of a single hue”—is among the most famous in all of Chinese parallel prose.

Bai Juyi (772–846), one of the great Tang poets; his Chang hen ge tells of the Xuanzong emperor’s doomed love for the consort Yang Guifei. Its closing couplet, which Xiong quoted—“Heaven is lasting and earth enduring, yet a time will come when both are gone; but this regret runs on and on, and will never reach an end”—is proverbial. Song of the Pipa is another of Bai’s long narrative poems.

Classical ci lyrics were composed to fixed metrical patterns, each named for a “tune-title” (cipai) that fixed the number and length of the lines and the placing of the rhymes. So “Southern Song,” “Fisherman’s Song,” “Partridge Sky,” and “Recalling the Maid of Qin” are verse forms, not subjects.

ch05.anchor: a traitor risen within the Party
ch05.note: Gu Shunzhang, who ran the Special Branch’s own operations and knew its every secret, defected to the Nationalists in April 1931 and forced the Party to abandon its Shanghai premises overnight—the disaster that closed the Yunnan Road safe house. His betrayal and its aftermath fill later chapters.
Yuan Mei (1716–1798), a leading poet and essayist of the Qing, known for verse of feeling and spontaneity and for holding that a poem should speak the writer’s own nature.

The West Hunan–Hubei (Xiang–E–Xi) Soviet base, on the lakes and marshes around Honghu, was built by He Long from 1928; it fell to the Nationalists’ “encirclement and suppression” campaigns in 1932. Xiong Jinding and Zhu Duanshou were posted there when the Shanghai organ closed.

ch05.anchor: the Zhou residence on Rue Massenet
ch05.note: In 1946 Zhou Enlai led the Communist delegation in Shanghai during the failing Nationalist–Communist negotiations; his residence and office at 107 Rue Massenet (today 73 Sinan Road) is preserved as the “Zhou Residence” museum.

ch05.anchor: Fourth Plenum of the Sixth Central Committee in January 1931
ch05.note: The Fourth Plenum of the Sixth Central Committee (January 1931), at which the Moscow-trained group around Wang Ming took hold of the Party. Here it serves only to date how long the Yunnan Road organ went undetected—more than two years.

ch05.anchor: Wu Jieping brought in to treat him as well
ch05.note: Wu Jieping (1917–2011), a renowned urologist who attended many of the Party’s leaders; that Zhou Enlai sent him marks the regard in which the dying Xiong Jinding was held.

The “Gang of Four”—Jiang Qing (Mao’s wife), Zhang Chunqiao, Yao Wenyuan, and Wang Hongwen—were the radical leaders who drove the Cultural Revolution and, in its last years, worked against the ailing Zhou Enlai. They were arrested a month after Mao’s death in 1976.

The “Horse Day” Incident of May 21, 1927: ma, “horse,” was the telegraph code for the twenty-first of the month. Nationalist officers in Changsha crushed the Communist-led peasant and labor unions in a bloody purge—one of the opening blows of the 1927 terror, and the moment that drove many Hunan revolutionaries, Xiong and Zhu among them, underground.

Shili yangchang, “the ten-li foreign market,” was the stock epithet for Shanghai’s foreign concessions—ten li of gaslit, moneyed, half-Western streets that stood for the whole glittering and treacherous city.

The detail is the source's and is faithful: in traditional Chinese medicine, repeated yawning is read as an early sign of a chill (zhaoliang), a symptom of the body's yang being caught off guard. Xiong Jinding, trained in Chinese medicine, takes his own yawning for proof he has caught cold and so has a pretext to register as a patient.

ch06.note: Tu Zuochao (1903–1988), a Hunan carpenter who trained as a wireless mechanic in the Soviet Union and became one of the Party’s first radio technicians; his codename “Carpenter” came from his boyhood trade. The chapter title, “It Was Not Me, It Was the Wind,” plays on the book’s conceit for radio work — the Communists as “windtalkers” who chase, listen for, and catch the wind of the airwaves. Corroborated in the Party-history literature.

Sandaotou, literally “three stripes,” was Shanghai slang for the patrolmen of the French Concession police, after the three braids or chevrons on their sleeves. The “tiger skin” a line later is the uniform itself: a stock image for borrowed official authority, as a lesser beast might dress in a tiger’s hide.

Yangjingbang English, named for a filled-in creek that once divided the foreign settlements, was the improvised trade-English of the Shanghai waterfront — a mix of English words, Chinese grammar, and coinages that outsiders found hard to follow. Here it is part of the painter’s disguise.

The Sixth National Congress of the Chinese Communist Party met from June to July 1928 outside Moscow — the only Party congress held abroad. After the Nationalist purges of 1927 no venue in China was safe, so delegates were smuggled to the Soviet Union. It is the setting in which several figures of this chapter first crossed paths.

ch06.anchor: Moscow's University of the East struck Tu Zuochao
ch06.note: The Communist University of the Toilers of the East (KUTV), founded in Moscow in 1921 to train revolutionaries from Asia; many early CCP cadres passed through it. The “International Wireless Training Class” mentioned here was one of its technical courses.

The Cheka (from the Russian initials for the “Extraordinary Commission”) was the Soviet political police founded in 1917; by 1929 its functions had passed to the OGPU, but the old name stuck in common speech. The station at Vladivostok served the Soviet Far East.

ch06.anchor: came to the revolution through New Youth
ch06.note: New Youth (Xin Qingnian, also published under the French title La Jeunesse), edited by Chen Duxiu, was the seminal magazine of the New Culture and May Fourth movements from 1915; it carried the first Chinese expositions of Marxism and drew a generation, Li Qiang among them, toward the Party.

Lord Mengchang (died 279 BCE), a noble of the Warring States kingdom of Qi, was famous for keeping some three thousand retainers of every description and standing by them; his name became a byword for open-handed, risk-taking patronage. Xia Yan means that Cai Shuhou sheltered the hunted as such a patron would.

The “4-12” is the coup of April 12, 1927, when Chiang Kai-shek’s forces, with Green Gang gunmen, turned on their Communist allies in Shanghai and massacred them — the event that opened the White Terror and drove the Party underground.

Xia Yan (1900–1995), pen name of Shen Naixi, was a leading left-wing playwright, screenwriter, and journalist, later a vice-minister of culture in the People’s Republic. His memoir Lazily Seeking Old Dreams is a standard source on the Shanghai underground’s cultural world.

An illuminated news display — letters spelled out by rows of electric bulbs and run in sequence — mounted on the roof of the Great World amusement arcade, an early piece of Shanghai’s electric spectacle.

The “Hao cipher” (Haomi) took its name from Zhou Enlai’s Party codename Wuhao. It combined transposition of the Chinese commercial telegraph code with a letter-to-figure substitution, was never reused, and was reckoned all but unbreakable; the Nationalists are said never to have read it. Deng Yingchao, Zhou’s wife, was its first cipher clerk.

The observatory at Xujiahui — known in the Republican period by its older French-Jesuit name, Zikawei — was founded by Jesuits in 1872 and was the great weather and time-signal station of the China coast; its forecasts, broadcast on long wave, were what Zhang Shenchuan practiced copying.

Two tortures of the period. On the “tiger bench” (laohudeng) the victim was tied seated with legs held flat while bricks were forced under the ankles, bending the knees backward to breaking. The “duckling’s paddle” (ya’er fushui) was a form of forced near-drowning. Both were standard in Nationalist police cells.

ch06.anchor: in the shape of the Eight Trigrams
ch06.note: The Eight Trigrams (bagua) are the eight three-line figures of the Book of Changes, traditionally arranged in a ring. The prison’s radial plan set nine cell-blocks around a central watch-pavilion, so that a few guards could oversee every corridor — a Chinese cousin of the panopticon. The blocks were named for the trigrams and the virtues: Heaven, Earth, Man, Sun, Moon, Star, Wisdom, Benevolence, Courage.

Yun Daiying (1895–1931), a founder of the Socialist Youth League and one of the Party’s most beloved teachers of the young, was arrested in 1930 and, once Gu Shunzhang’s defection exposed him, executed at the Central Military Prison in April 1931 at thirty-six. His prison quatrain, quoted here, circulated widely among the inmates. Corroborated.

“Captive of Chu” (Chu qiu) alludes to Zhong Yi, a musician of Chu held prisoner in Jin who kept his home dress and home music and never bent, recorded in the Zuo Zhuan; it came to mean a captive who keeps his dignity and his loyalties intact. Yun Daiying casts himself so.

Labor University (Laoda), founded at Jiangwan in 1927, tried to fuse study with manual work in the spirit of the worker-study movement, and carried a strong anarchist strain; its patrons included the KMT elders Cai Yuanpei, Wu Zhihui, Li Shizeng, and Zhang Jingjiang. It was closed in 1932.

Zhou Libo (1908–1979) became one of the People’s Republic’s most celebrated novelists; his land-reform novel The Hurricane won a Stalin Prize, and Great Changes in a Mountain Village chronicled collectivization. Here he is a fellow student expelled with Su Gangda.

Liu Renjing (1902–1987) was one of the dozen or so delegates to the Party’s founding First Congress in 1921 and first head of its youth league; he later became a Trotskyist, which is why he is among the “penitents” here rather than in the Party’s pantheon.

Cao Diqiu (1909–1976) rose after 1949 to be mayor of Shanghai; he was hounded to his death during the Cultural Revolution. The parenthetical string of names and dates in this passage is the author’s own roll-call of the notables the Reformatory happened to hold.

Liao Zhongkai (1877–1925) was the left-Nationalist leader and financier of the first KMT–CCP alliance, assassinated in 1925. His son-in-law Li Shaoshi worked in the underground and was shot dead in Chongqing in 1945 in a still-disputed incident.

“Granny Xia,” Huang Youmei (1870–1944), was the mother-in-law of the martyr Zhao Shiyan (executed 1927) and mother of Xia Zhixu; she sheltered underground workers for years and was honored in the Party’s memory as a “revolutionary mother.”

Both went on to eminence in the arts: Zhang Ding (1917–2010) as a designer and painter who helped shape the national emblem and much official art, Ling Zifeng (1917–1999) as a leading film director. In 1936 they were young men in the Reformatory.

ch06.anchor: sham CCP general secretary Xiang Zhongfa
ch06.note: Xiang Zhongfa (1880–1931) was the Party’s general secretary until his arrest and quick capitulation in June 1931; his story fills a later chapter. The word “sham” (wei) and the framing are the Nationalist booklet’s own; the author quotes them as evidence of what the “penitents” were made to read.

ch06.anchor: the Three Principles of the People
ch06.note: The Three Principles of the People (Sanmin zhuyi) — nationalism, democracy, and the people’s livelihood — were Sun Yat-sen’s doctrine and the official creed of the Nationalist state; to “propagate doctrines incompatible with” them was the standing charge against Communists.

Two of these names differ from the school’s own roster given earlier, where the same trainees appear as Feng Yiping and He Shida. The divergence is in the sources — the newspaper worked from police-blotter names, themselves partly the prisoners’ false confessions — and is left as printed.

Su Gangda’s little verse of paired four-character lines doubles as a coded farewell to smuggle out to his family: its last line, gaowei qinren, mingtian zaijian — “give comfort to your kin; till we meet again tomorrow” — supplies this section’s title and reads, in the mouth of a condemned man, as a promise past death.
