ch06.anchor: Sixteen trainees in all gathered at the Welfare Electric Company
ch06.note: The author's headcounts for the training school do not quite square, and are reproduced as printed. Sixteen trainees are named here as the full enrollment; the raid scene below counts “eighteen trainees” present that afternoon; and the arrest tallies run to “the other twenty” and to seventeen-plus-three sentenced — figures that evidently fold in the instructors (Zhang Shenchuan, Zeng Hualun, Fang Tingzhen and others) and any who joined the class after this roll was taken. The discrepancy is the source's, not a slip of translation.

The conceit turns on feng (“wind”) for the airwaves: the radio men chase, listen for, and catch the wind. The Chinese word rendered “windtalkers,” fengyuzhe, is also the Chinese title of the 2002 war film Windtalkers, about the Navajo code-talkers of the Pacific war; the author is punning on it. No connection to the Navajo cipher is implied.

ch07.anchor: first proposed at the National Congress of Soviet Areas
ch07.note: The National Congress of Soviet Areas (全国苏维埃区域代表大会) gathered delegates from the Communist base areas and the Red Army in Shanghai in the spring of 1930. It resolved to convene a First National Soviet Congress, which duly met at Ruijin in November 1931 and founded the Chinese Soviet Republic. The event is well attested; its exact dates are not (see the note at “May 5, 1930”).

ch07.anchor: the ×× Party
ch07.note: In Ding Ling’s original the Communist Party could not be named in print under the censorship of the day, so it appears as “××.” The blanks stand for the Communist Party.

ch07.anchor: the writer Ding Ling in her
ch07.note: Ding Ling (1904–1986), one of the foremost women writers of the century and later a leading literary figure of the People’s Republic; her documentary sketch “Shanghai, Spring 1930” appeared that same year. Her husband, the writer Hu Yepin, is a subject of this chapter.

ch07.anchor: Xiong Shihui read over and over the words plainly set down there
ch07.note: Xiong Shihui (1893–1974), a Kuomintang general; at this time commander of the Shanghai–Wusong garrison and thus the “commander” of the chapter, later governor of Jiangxi. It was in that capacity that he directed the hunt for the congress.

ch07.anchor: assigned by Zhou Enlai as an assistant to the famous Soviet spy Sorge
ch07.note: Richard Sorge (1895–1944), the Soviet Union’s master intelligence agent in the Far East, who ran a network in Shanghai and later Tokyo; he was arrested in Japan in 1941 and hanged in 1944. Zhang Wenqiu’s claim to have assisted him is her own and is debated by historians. Her two daughters, Liu Siqi and Shaohua, married Mao Zedong’s sons Mao Anying and Mao Anqing — hence “Mao Zedong’s kinswoman by marriage.” The same Sorge network reappears at the chapter’s end through Ozaki Hotsumi.

ch07.anchor: was an alias used by Deng Fa in September 1937
ch07.note: Deng Fa (1906–1946), a Communist labor leader and, later, security chief; he died in the same 1946 plane crash as Ye Ting and Wang Ruofei. Here the author is weighing his sources: if “Fang Lin” really was Deng Fa, the dates do not fit, since in early 1930 Deng Fa held only provincial posts in Guangdong and Hong Kong and was in a Hong Kong jail. The identification is doubtful.

ch07.anchor: his own spear against his own shield
ch07.note: From the parable in the Han Feizi of the peddler who boasted at once of a shield nothing could pierce and a spear that would pierce anything, until a bystander asked what would happen if the one met the other. The Chinese word for “contradiction,” maodun, is literally “spear-shield.” The sense here is turning the enemy’s own ground and methods against him.

ch07.anchor: the great hermit who hides in the city
ch07.note: From a poem by the Jin-dynasty writer Wang Kangju: “The lesser hermit hides in the hills and marshes; the great hermit hides in the court and market.” True concealment is not flight to the wilderness but invisibility in the thick of the crowd — the conceit of the chapter’s title.

ch07.anchor: on Hart Road in the British Concession
ch07.note: Shanghai had no “British Concession”: the British and American settlements had merged in 1863 into the jointly administered International Settlement. The memoir sources loosely call it the “British Concession” because the Settlement was British-dominated. Hart Road lay in the Settlement’s western district, which is the author’s correction in the paragraph that follows.

ch07.anchor: "seventy-two tenants"
ch07.note: A stock phrase for a warren of a tenement crammed with poor households of every trade and temper, made proverbial by the comic play and film The Seventy-Two Tenants. The number is figurative, meaning “a great many.”

ch07.anchor: the anti-Japanese martyr Zhao Yiman
ch07.note: Zhao Yiman (1905–1936), born Li Kuntai, an organizer and commander of the anti-Japanese resistance in Manchuria. Captured wounded in November 1935, she endured months of torture and was executed by the Japanese near Zhuhe (today Shangzhi, Heilongjiang) in August 1936. Her farewell letter to her young son, quoted here, is among the best-known texts of the resistance; the 1950 film Zhao Yiman made her a household name. Well attested.

ch07.anchor: carried a Mauser
ch07.note: The Mauser C96, the broom-handled semi-automatic pistol that the Chinese called the “box cannon” (hezipao); with its detachable wooden holster-stock it was the favored sidearm of the Special Branch’s action men.

ch07.anchor: the concessions' Municipal Council and French Municipal Council
ch07.note: The two concession governments: the Shanghai Municipal Council (gongbuju), which ran the International Settlement, and the French Municipal Council (gongdongju), which ran the French Concession. Each kept its own police, courts, and prisons.

ch07.anchor: was a product of Li Lisan's
ch07.note: The “Li Lisan line” was the ultra-left course that briefly dominated the Party in mid-1930, ordering armed uprisings in the great cities on the belief that a nationwide revolutionary high tide was at hand. It was checked at the enlarged Third Plenum in September 1930 and repudiated soon after. Li Lisan himself long outlived it.

ch07.anchor: Red May drew nearer by the day
ch07.note: “Red May” (hong wuyue) was the revolutionary calendar’s crowded month of commemorations — May Day and the memorial days of the movement’s dead — a season of heightened Communist activity and, in answer, heightened repression.

ch07.anchor: hung with the sickle-and-axe flag
ch07.note: The earliest Chinese Communist flags bore a crossed sickle and axe (lian-dao fu-tou), the axe standing for the industrial worker; the design was later standardized as the sickle and hammer of the international movement.

ch07.anchor: I told Ozaki about it and asked him to help
ch07.note: Ozaki Hotsumi (1901–1944), correspondent of the Asahi Shimbun and a noted authority on China, sympathetic to the Communist cause. He was a key member of Richard Sorge’s Soviet spy ring; arrested in 1941, he was hanged in 1944, the same year as Sorge. The two men’s appearance at either end of this chapter — Sorge above, Ozaki here — is a genuine crossing of the threads.

ch07.anchor: At about nine on the morning of May 5, 1930
ch07.note: The book here dates the congress to May 5–7, but on the preceding pages it quotes Zhang Wenqiu (May 20) and Hong Yangsheng without a date. The dates generally accepted in the scholarship are May 20–23, 1930. The sources genuinely disagree, and the account is left as the author gives it.

ch07.anchor: Even Lord Guan, he said, lost Maicheng
ch07.note: Two proverbial defeats from the Romance of the Three Kingdoms: Guan Yu (“Lord Guan”) was cornered and killed after the fall of Maicheng, and Zhuge Liang (“Kongming”) lost the strategic pass of Jieting through a subordinate’s blunder. To invoke them is to say that even the greatest commanders suffer a reverse.

ch07.anchor: along with Rou Shi, Feng Keng, and others
ch07.note: Rou Shi (1902–1931) and Feng Keng (1907–1931) were two of the “Five Martyrs of the League of Left-Wing Writers,” young writers arrested and secretly shot by the Kuomintang at Longhua, Shanghai, in February 1931. Lu Xun mourned them in his essay “In Memory of the Forgotten.” Hu Yepin was a third of the five.

ch07.anchor: walked the Long March
ch07.note: The Long March (1934–1936) was the Red Army’s fighting retreat of some six thousand miles from its encircled base areas in the southeast to the far northwest, under constant Nationalist pursuit. The ordeal cost most of the marchers their lives, confirmed Mao Zedong as the Party’s paramount leader, and became the founding epic of Chinese Communism.

ch07.anchor: took part in the Revolution of 1911
ch07.note: The Revolution of 1911 (the Xinhai Revolution) overthrew the Qing dynasty and ended more than two thousand years of imperial rule, founding the Republic of China the following year. It opened with the Wuchang Uprising (see Chapter One).

ch07.anchor: very powerful in Hongkou
ch07.note: Hongkou, the district north of Suzhou Creek, was the part of the International Settlement where the Japanese population and businesses concentrated; in practice it was Shanghai’s Japanese quarter, and Japanese-run premises there lay effectively beyond the reach of the Settlement’s own police.

ch07.anchor: changed into qipao and silk stockings and added gold and silver jewelry
ch07.note: The qipao (also known as the cheongsam), the close-fitting, high-collared one-piece dress that in 1930s Shanghai was the mark of a fashionable, modern woman.

ch07.anchor: a great golden character shou
ch07.note: Shou, the character for “long life,” is the emblem at the heart of a Chinese birthday celebration, hung large and gilded; the longevity peaches, long-life noodles, and Buddha’s-hand citrons set out around it all carry the same wish for the honoree’s long life.

ch07.anchor: even Kongming lost Jieting.
ch07.note: A companion to the Lord Guan proverb just above, from the same Three Kingdoms lore: Zhuge Liang, styled Kongming, the age’s model strategist, lost the vital pass of Jieting after entrusting it to the overconfident Ma Su, and was forced into retreat. The sense: even a genius is not spared his defeats.

ch08.anchor: the seventeenth year of the Republic
ch08.note: The Republic of China numbered its years from its founding in 1912, so the seventeenth year of the Republic was 1928.

ch08.anchor: the Carnegie Institute of Technology in America he had read business management
ch08.note: The source writes Kangnaijie gongye daxue (康奈杰工业大学), given here as the Carnegie Institute of Technology, the engineering school in Pittsburgh (today part of Carnegie Mellon University). The two accounts in this passage disagree on what Xu Enzeng studied there: Zou Taofen recalls electrical engineering, Xu Enzeng’s own memoir business management.

ch08.anchor: classmate of Zou Taofen's the whole way
ch08.note: Zou Taofen (1895–1944), a celebrated progressive journalist and publisher, editor of Shenghuo (“Life”) Weekly and founder of the Life Bookstore, and one of the “Seven Gentlemen” jailed in 1936 for urging resistance to Japan. That the future head of the Kuomintang’s secret police had been his schoolmate, and then set agents to shadow him for years, is the irony the author is pointing to.

ch08.anchor: nor for her unbound natural feet
ch08.note: “Natural feet” (tianzu) meant feet never bound — a badge of the new, educated woman and of the movement against foot-binding, but still an oddity to an older generation. That Qian Zhuangfei’s mother disapproved of her son’s bride for her unbound feet places the family on the near side of a great social change.

ch08.anchor: his kinsman Qian Xuantong
ch08.note: Qian Xuantong (1887–1939), a leading philologist and iconoclast of the New Culture movement and a champion of the written vernacular. It was his prodding — the famous exchange about whether it was worth rousing the sleepers in a windowless “iron house” — that moved Lu Xun to write A Madman’s Diary (1918), the first Western-style story in vernacular Chinese, for the magazine New Youth.

ch08.anchor: the Wuyue kings Qian Liu and Qian Chu
ch08.note: Wuyue (907–978) was one of the kingdoms of the Five Dynasties period, centered on Hangzhou; Qian Liu was its founder and Qian Chu its last king, who yielded peacefully to the Song. The surname Qian (钱) is common in the region, and descent from its royal house a point of local pride.

ch08.anchor: the late film star Li Lili
ch08.note: Li Lili (1915–2005), born Qian Zhenzhen, a daughter of Qian Zhuangfei, was one of the brightest stars of 1930s Chinese cinema (Playthings, The Big Road, Daybreak); she took her stage surname from her mentor, the songwriter Li Jinhui. The album spoken of at the chapter’s close was her memoir in pictures.

ch08.anchor: the "local spy," the "inside spy,"
ch08.note: The five classes of agent from the last chapter, “The Use of Spies,” of Sun Tzu’s Art of War: the local spy (a native of the enemy’s country), the inside spy (an enemy official suborned), the double or converted spy (the enemy’s agent turned back on him), the doomed or expendable spy (fed false information to carry to the enemy, at the cost of his life), and the surviving or living spy (who comes back with intelligence).

ch08.anchor: the 'Three Heroes of Longtan' are household names now
ch08.note: The “Three Heroes of Longtan” (龙潭三杰) — Qian Zhuangfei, Li Kenong, and Hu Di — are the three Communist agents who penetrated the Kuomintang’s intelligence service, the subject of this chapter. Longtan, “dragon’s pool,” echoes the set phrase longtan huxue, “the dragon’s pool and the tiger’s den” — the enemy’s innermost lair. The epithet is traditionally credited to Zhou Enlai.

ch08.anchor: to run the West Lake Exposition
ch08.note: The West Lake Exposition of 1929, held at Hangzhou over some four months, was one of Republican China’s largest national exhibitions, showcasing industry, agriculture, art, and education.

ch08.anchor: sending Nie Rongzhen to Gu Shunzhang's side
ch08.note: Nie Rongzhen (1899–1992), later one of the ten marshals of the People’s Republic; here he is moved into the Central Special Branch to keep the increasingly wayward Gu Shunzhang in check. His daughter Nie Li, quoted just below, became a lieutenant general and a leader of China’s defense-technology programs.

ch08.anchor: an attempt to assassinate Chiang Kai-shek
ch08.note: Whether Gu Shunzhang’s months of magic shows in Wuhan really screened a plot to kill Chiang Kai-shek is uncertain. The claim rests on the Kuomintang intelligence files used by Wakeman; the Communist sources quoted here treat the Wuhan sojourn rather as Gu’s self-indulgent dawdling. The author leaves the two readings standing side by side, as he found them.

ch08.anchor: the Central Plains War among Chiang
ch08.note: The Central Plains War (1930) was the largest of the warlord conflicts of the Nanjing decade, pitting Chiang Kai-shek against a coalition led by Yan Xishan, Feng Yuxiang, and Li Zongren. Chiang’s victory that autumn freed him to turn his armies on the Communist base areas — the campaigns that follow.

ch08.anchor: was the beginning of the First
ch08.note: The first of five “encirclement and suppression” campaigns (1930–1934) that Chiang Kai-shek mounted against the Central Soviet base in Jiangxi. The first four were beaten off; the fifth, in 1934, forced the Red Army out on the Long March. The Communists’ advance knowledge of the enemy’s plans, supplied by Qian Zhuangfei and his fellows, helped defeat the first two.

ch08.anchor: Zhu (De), Mao (Zedong), Peng (Dehuai)
ch08.note: The four commanders on whose heads Chiang set a fifty-thousand-yuan bounty: Zhu De (1886–1976), commander-in-chief of the Red Army; Mao Zedong (1893–1976); Peng Dehuai (1898–1974); and Huang Gonglüe (1898–1931), a corps commander killed in action the next year. The source names them by surname alone, as the leaflet did.

ch08.anchor: I fancy some bang-bang chicken
ch08.note: Bang-bang chicken (bangbang ji) is a Sichuan cold dish of poached chicken torn into shreds under a spicy sesame dressing; the name is said to come from the wooden club once used to pound the meat tender.

ch08.anchor: the Horse King has three eyes
ch08.note: “The Horse King has three eyes” (Ma Wangye you san zhi yan) is a proverbial boast — roughly, “I’ll show him I’m not to be trifled with.” The Horse King, a folk deity, is shown with a third eye in his brow; to make a man “know” it is to make him feel one’s power.

ch08.anchor: the *Collected Works of Zeng Wenzheng*
ch08.note: Zeng Guofan (1811–1872), posthumously titled Zeng Wenzheng, was the Qing statesman and general who broke the Taiping Rebellion; his collected works stood on every literate household’s shelf. Keying a cipher to a widely owned book — a “book code” — gave sender and receiver a shared key that raised no suspicion.

ch08.anchor: crossed the Wu River southward
ch08.note: The Wu (Wujiang), the great northern tributary of the Yangtze in Guizhou, crossed and recrossed by the Central Red Army during the Long March. Qian Zhuangfei died near it in the spring of 1935 — the death Zhou Enlai recalled at the Chongqing dinner with which this chapter opened.

ch08.anchor: sent agents to murder him
ch08.note: How Qian Zhuangfei died is disputed. The older accounts have him killed by a local anti-Communist militia, or by bandits, after he was separated from the column during an air raid near Jinsha, Guizhou, on April 1, 1935; Wang Zhitao’s later suggestion, given here, that Chiang had him assassinated is a minority view resting on inference. What is not in doubt is that he was murdered — bound and stabbed — at about the age of forty, and that his body was found days afterward.

ch08.anchor: from the Western Route Army
ch08.note: The Western Route Army was the Red Army force of some twenty thousand that crossed the Yellow River into the Gansu corridor in late 1936 and was all but destroyed by Muslim cavalry over the winter of 1936–37; the survivors straggled back to Yan’an. Ouyang Yi was among them.

ch08.anchor: His account is borne out by Meng Zhen
ch08.note: The block quotation is cited to a 1999 volume by Yang Yingqi and Zhang Wandong, which reprints the memoir of Zhang Guodong, the former Investigation Section trainee whose recollections the author leans on throughout this chapter; the author treats the quoted passage as Zhang Guodong's own account, and it is reproduced as printed.

ch08.anchor: escorted toward the Eyuwan Soviet
ch08.note: The Eyuwan Soviet was a Communist rural base area on the borders of Hubei, Henan, and Anhui provinces, its name built from those provinces’ one-character abbreviations (E–Yu–Wan). A “Soviet” here means such a base — a revolutionary government on the Russian model — not the USSR.

ch08.anchor: as interpreter for Li De
ch08.note: “Li De” was the Chinese name of Otto Braun (1900–1974), the German Comintern military adviser to the Central Soviet, whose rigid, textbook tactics are widely blamed for the defeat that forced the Long March. Rendered as a Chinese name, he is easy to miss for a foreigner.

ch08.anchor: 'Nanshe' in Beiping
ch08.note: The Nanshe (“Southern Society”) was an influential literary society founded in 1909, its members largely revolutionary intellectuals hostile to the Qing. “Beiping” is the name Beijing carried from 1928 to 1949, while the national capital was at Nanjing.

ch08.anchor: star pupil of Nanyang College
ch08.note: Nanyang Public School (Nanyang College), founded in Shanghai in 1896, was one of China’s first modern institutions of higher learning and the forerunner of today’s Jiao Tong University.

ch08.anchor: broke his cauldrons and sank his boats
ch08.note: A classical idiom (po fu chen zhou): in 207 BC the warlord Xiang Yu, having crossed a river to give battle, sank his boats and smashed his cooking pots so that his soldiers knew there was no retreat and no meal but victory. To burn one’s bridges and stake everything on a single throw.

ch08.anchor: nine streams and three teachings
ch08.note: A set phrase (san jiao jiu liu, “the three teachings and the nine streams”): once the three doctrines — Confucian, Daoist, Buddhist — and the nine classical schools of thought, now every sort and station of people, high and low alike.

ch09.anchor: then chairman of the CCP Central Politburo and of its Standing Committee
ch09.note: Xiang Zhongfa (1880–1931), the man this chapter is about. A Wuhan dockworker and boatman turned union organizer, he was raised up at the Party’s 1928 Sixth Congress to nominal head of the Party, a proletarian figurehead; real authority lay with Li Lisan, and then with the Moscow-backed Wang Ming group and the Comintern. Gu Shunzhang’s defection in April 1931 exposed him, and he was seized in Shanghai on June 22, 1931, and shot within days. Whether he broke under interrogation is the question the chapter weighs. The standard accounts, and the Party’s own later verdict (Deng Yingchao, 1988, endorsed by Chen Yun), hold that he confessed at once and gave up his comrades; a dissenting minority (Zhang Ji’en) argued the confession was a forgery. His arrest and execution are not in doubt; what the sources here contest is the extent of his betrayal.

ch09.anchor: Huang Mulan has told us a story
ch09.note: Huang Mulan (1907–2017), an underground Communist courier and liaison in early-1930s Shanghai, later a businesswoman in Hong Kong and, after 1949, a prisoner for many years before her rehabilitation. Her long life and her 2012 memoir made her a celebrated figure, marketed as the “most beautiful red agent.” Her account of Xiang Zhongfa’s capture — that she overheard it by chance in a café — is the version the author sets out to test in this chapter, and treats throughout as an interested, self-flattering source. Her portrait appears below.

ch09.anchor: saving of Zhou Enlai and Guan Xiangying
ch09.note: Guan Xiangying (1902–1946), a Manchu Communist and youth and labor organizer, later political commissar of the 120th Division of the Eighth Route Army. Here he is simply the imprisoned comrade Huang Mulan was tasked with helping to free.

ch09.anchor: a film at the Grand
ch09.note: The Grand Theater (Da Guangming), a landmark cinema on Bubbling Well Road; its Art Deco building, remodeled in 1933 by the architect László Hudec, was among the grandest picture houses in East Asia.

ch09.anchor: a heroine in the mold of Hua Mulan
ch09.note: Hua Mulan, the legendary woman warrior of the old Ballad of Mulan, who disguised herself as a man to take her aged father’s place in the army. Huang Mulan’s given name, Mulan (慕兰, “admiring Mulan”), is drawn from her — the point of the wordplay in this passage.

ch09.anchor: as for *Dream of the Red Chamber*
ch09.note: Two of the great classical Chinese novels: Romance of the Three Kingdoms, a sweeping historical war epic, and Dream of the Red Chamber, an intimate novel of a declining gentry house and its doomed romance. Huang Mulan offers her taste for the martial epic over the domestic romance as proof of her “masculine” temper.

ch09.anchor: publicly announced by Dong Biwu
ch09.note: Dong Biwu (1886–1975), a founder of the Chinese Communist Party and a delegate to its First Congress in 1921; after 1949 he became a vice-chairman of the People’s Republic and, for a time, its acting head of state.

ch09.anchor: married Wan Xiyan
ch09.note: Wan Xiyan (1900–1928), a Communist organizer and propagandist, Huang Mulan’s second husband; he was killed in 1928 leading a peasant force against the town of Wan’an in Jiangxi.

ch09.anchor: was He Chang, a member of the Sixth Central Committee
ch09.note: He Chang (1906–1935), a Communist labor and military-political leader, Huang Mulan’s third husband; he died during the Long March.

ch09.anchor: Chen Zhigao invited me for coffee
ch09.note: Chen Zhigao, a Shanghai lawyer and the son of a judge of the Mixed Court, who used his father’s name and his own connections to win the release of arrested comrades, and who later married Huang Mulan.

ch09.anchor: a student at Aurora University in Shanghai
ch09.note: The Université l’Aurore (Zhendan), a French Jesuit university in Shanghai’s French Concession, known for its law and medical faculties.

ch09.anchor: the North China Political Security Bureau
ch09.note: The Communist clandestine security and counter-intelligence network in the Beiping–Tianjin region, set up by Chen Geng after the Shanghai apparatus was blown. (Beiping was the name of Beijing from 1928 to 1949.)

ch09.anchor: the "Moskvin" of the Comintern department's report
ch09.note: “Moskvin” was Zhou Enlai’s codename in his dealings with the Comintern; the report’s reference to “Comrade Mo(skvin)” directing the reorganized special-work apparatus is thus a veiled naming of Zhou himself.

ch09.anchor: the Metropole Hotel and lie low for a time
ch09.note: The Metropole Hotel (Ducheng Fandian), a foreign-run hotel; the leaders’ brazen arrival in business dress, as the account has it, was itself the cover.

ch09.anchor: No. 44 Yong'anli on North Sichuan Road
ch09.note: A shikumen lane house in Hongkou used as one of Zhou Enlai’s Shanghai safe houses, now preserved as a memorial to his underground years. The author cites its later designation to press his point that Zhou would not still have been living there sixteen hours after Xiang’s arrest.

ch09.anchor: through Bao Wenwei, Wu Xingya
ch09.note: Bao Wenwei (1902–1991), a scholar of French literature who, under Special Branch direction, penetrated the Songhu Garrison Command as its French interpreter; he later became a university professor and the Chinese translator of Rabelais. His family’s account and Pan Hannian’s differ on the dates of his service, a discrepancy the author probes at length here.

ch09.anchor: his mother He Xiangning
ch09.note: He Xiangning (1878–1972), a revolutionary, painter, and widow of the Nationalist leader Liao Zhongkai; her son Liao Chengzhi (1908–1983), a Communist jailed at various times by both sides, rose after 1949 to senior posts in overseas-Chinese and foreign affairs.

ch09.anchor: the Hanyeping Company's ship No. 180
ch09.note: The Han-Ye-Ping Coal and Iron Company — the Hanyang ironworks, the Daye iron mines, and the Pingxiang colliery combined — was China’s first large modern iron-and-steel enterprise, centered on the Wuhan region where Xiang Zhongfa began as a worker.

ch09.anchor: the great Jinghan Railway workers' strike
ch09.note: The February 1923 strike on the Beijing–Hankou (Jinghan) Railway, crushed by the warlord Wu Peifu in the “February Seventh Massacre,” was a landmark and a bloody defeat for the early Communist-led labor movement.

ch09.anchor: Luo Zhanglong describes the Sixth Congress
ch09.note: Luo Zhanglong (1896–1995), one of the earliest Communist labor leaders; he broke with the leadership over the Fourth Plenum of 1931 and was expelled, which colors his memoir of these years.

ch09.anchor: Mif took his place
ch09.note: Pavel Mif, a Comintern official and rector of Sun Yat-sen University in Moscow, was the patron of Wang Ming and the Moscow-trained “Returned Students” (the “Twenty-eight Bolsheviks”). Luo Zhanglong’s account shows him installing Xiang Zhongfa as Party Secretary on Stalin’s instructions, to visibly muted applause.

ch09.anchor: those stood for the two most fashionable cuts
ch09.note: The joke turns on the shop-sign words Su-Guang-Cheng: Su for Suzhou, Guang for Guangdong (Canton), chengyi for ready-made clothes. “Suguangcheng” is not one shop’s name but the generic label “Suzhou-and-Cantonese tailoring,” so it hangs on more signboards than any other — which is also why the sources cannot agree whether Xiang’s safe house was the Suguangcheng grain shop or the Suguangcheng tailor shop.

ch09.anchor: Yang Hu, to negotiate
ch09.note: Yang Hu (1889–1966), a Green Gang-connected Nationalist general and Shanghai garrison commander, a principal enforcer of Chiang Kai-shek’s April 1927 purge of the Communists in the city.

ch09.anchor: then at Mount Lu, received the first urgent telegram
ch09.note: Mount Lu (Lushan) in Jiangxi, a cool highland resort that served as Chiang Kai-shek’s summer headquarters; from here he directed the Encirclement campaigns against the Communist base areas.

ch09.anchor: Kuomintang Zhongtong publication *The Turn* carries
ch09.note: The Turn (Zhuanbian) was an internal Zhongtong compilation of recantations by Communist defectors. The “Report of the Former Bogus CCP General Secretary Xiang Zhongfa” in its appendix — his so-called Confession — is the disputed document at the center of this chapter’s argument.

ch09.anchor: the Youth League General Secretary Qin Bangxian
ch09.note: Qin Bangxian (1907–1946), better known as Bo Gu, one of the Moscow-trained “Twenty-eight Bolsheviks”; within months he would head the Party’s Provisional Center.

ch09.anchor: Volume Eleven of the *Shilüe Gaoben*
ch09.note: The Shilüe Gaoben (Draft Chronicle) is the vast day-by-day compilation drawn from Chiang Kai-shek’s papers and diaries. The author’s discovery there of Chiang’s June 23 telegram ordering Xiang Zhongfa shot is the chapter’s clinching evidence: the “secret cable” whose very existence the section title disputes did, corroborated in Chiang’s own record, exist.

ch10.anchor: a cold wind and a bitter rain
ch10.note: The chapter opens on a four-part play on the Chinese figures that pair wind with rain. Chen Duxiu’s years were hufeng-huanyu, “summoning wind and rain,” commanding events at will; Qu Qiubai’s brief tenure a “violent storm”; Xiang Zhongfa’s a “foul wind and bloody rain,” a reign of terror; and Bo Gu’s a qifeng-kuyu, a “cold wind and bitter rain,” the set phrase for wretched, comfortless times.

Ruijin, a town in southern Jiangxi, was the seat of the Central Revolutionary Base, or Central Soviet — the largest of the Communist rural bases and, from November 1931, capital of the self-proclaimed Chinese Soviet Republic. It was the destination of the underground courier lines this chapter describes, and the starting point, in 1934, of the Long March.

Zhang Wentian (1900–1976), who wrote under the name Luo Fu, one of the Moscow-trained “Twenty-eight Bolsheviks.” He took over as the Party’s general secretary in early 1935, after the Zunyi conference, and later served as a diplomat and vice foreign minister.
Qin Guan (1049–1100), styled Shaoyou, a major lyric (ci) poet of the Northern Song and one of the disciples gathered around Su Shi. The line of descent is the Qin family’s own claim.

Qin Jin (1467–1544), styled Fengshan, a high official under the Ming Jiajing emperor. The family phrase renders his career: he headed five of the boards across the Ming’s two capitals, Beijing and Nanjing (each kept a parallel set of Six Boards), and rose to the honorary rank of Grand Guardian (taibao). The Jichang Garden his family laid out survives in Wuxi as one of the country’s celebrated classical gardens.
Qin Jiacong (English name Frank Ching), a journalist and a descendant of the same Wuxi Qin line, whose family history traces the clan across some nine centuries.

An echo of the May Fourth attack on Confucian ritualism — the “rites that eat people” of Lu Xun’s Diary of a Madman (1918). Bo Gu, writing here as “Shanglin” in 1925, was a student caught up in that iconoclasm.

ch10.anchor: bleak and forlorn and steeped in grief
ch10.note: The phrase is Li Qingzhao’s, the opening reduplicatives of her famous song lyric “Note After Note” (Sheng sheng man) — a byword in Chinese for desolate grief.

“Changlin” is Bo Gu, whom his mother knew by his childhood name; the memoirist Qin Moya is his eldest daughter. Bo Gu died on April 8, 1946, in the air crash at Heicha Mountain in Xingxian, Shanxi, that killed a group of Party leaders returning from the Chongqing talks — the “April 8 martyrs.” His mother, kept in the dark, went on waiting for him.

Huarun, in English China Resources, grew out of the Party’s underground trading network described in this chapter; today it is a state-owned conglomerate among the Fortune Global 500. Qin Bangli (1908–1968), Bo Gu’s younger brother, ran it under the alias Yang Lin; the chapter follows him from a Wuxi money house to the founding of the firm.

The Sino-French Drugstore (Zhongfa Yaofang) was a well-known Western-style pharmacy chain in Republican Shanghai; a branch in the treaty port of Shantou, in eastern Guangdong, gave the Party a respectable commercial front and a waystation on the sea route south.

ch10.anchor: escorted several hundred comrades in all through enemy-held territory
ch10.note: The names that follow are a roll-call of the men who would run the People’s Republic — among them Zhou Enlai, Deng Xiaoping, Liu Shaoqi, and Hu Yaobang, and the future marshals Ye Jianying, Liu Bocheng, and Nie Rongzhen — passed one by one along this single courier line into the Jiangxi base.

ch10.anchor: took the train on to Shaoyang
ch10.note: Shaoyang is in central Hunan, far off this Guangdong-to-Fujian route; the name as printed in the Biography of Chen Yun is almost certainly a slip, most likely for a place near Shantou. —Trans.

ch10.anchor: chief of the executive section of the Central Political Security Bureau
ch10.note: The Central Political Security Bureau, formed in 1931, was the security and counter-intelligence organ of the Jiangxi Soviet — a separate body from the Shanghai Special Branch, and a forerunner of the Party’s later state-security apparatus. It ran its own courier lines, which is the crux of the author’s argument here: the “Chen Pannian” of these accounts belongs to it and is not the famous Pan Hannian.

ch10.anchor: good at building a new one
ch10.note: Both slogans are Mao Zedong’s, from 1949. The first paraphrases “Farewell, Leighton Stuart” (August 1949), whose received text reads “Blockade us for eight or ten years and all of China’s problems will be solved”; the book gives “decades.” The second is from his opening address to the Chinese People’s Political Consultative Conference in September 1949, on the eve of the People’s Republic.

ch11.note: The Seventy-Two Tenants (Qishi’er jia fangke) is a classic Shanghai huaji comedy, a stage farce, later filmed, about the crowd of tenants packed into one ramshackle lane house, famous for its gallery of city types. The words filling this paragraph — niangyi, afei, biesan, baixiangren and the rest — are Shanghai and Wu-dialect street slang; the author lays them on to fix xiaokai in the same idiom of the 1930s city.

ch11.anchor: his early novel The Bitter Cup
ch11.note: The Bitter Cup (Kubei) was an early novel by Pan Hannian, who first made his name in Shanghai as a left-wing writer and editor before he turned to underground work. The scare-quoted phrases here are the novel’s own romantic-decadent language, which the author quotes with a dry smile.

The Zhongshan suit (after Sun Yat-sen, whose Chinese name was Sun Zhongshan; known in the West as the “Mao suit”) was the plain, semi-military tunic adopted by Chinese revolutionaries and later worn by the Republic’s officials. Because the Kuomintang left and the Communists favored it, wearing one could get a man branded “red.”

The “Left League” is the League of Left-Wing Writers (see the note at Chapter Seven); the “Dramatists’ League” is its sister body, the League of Left-Wing Dramatists. Both were Communist-led cultural fronts of the early 1930s, and Pan Hannian’s Party work in this period ran through them.

ch11.anchor: little Elisa, in The Wild Swans
ch11.note: Hans Christian Andersen’s tale The Wild Swans gives the chapter its title. Its heroine, Elisa, can free her eleven brothers — turned into swans by their stepmother the queen — only by weaving them shirts of nettles, and she may not speak a word until the task is done, on pain of their deaths. Her enforced silence is the author’s figure for the underground worker who can tell no one what he does.

The “CC Clique” was the Kuomintang faction built around the brothers Chen Guofu and Chen Lifu, which controlled the party’s organization apparatus and, through the Zhongtong (see the note at Chapter One), much of its secret-police and anti-Communist work.

ch11.anchor: Xu Minghong for the Nineteenth Route Army
ch11.note: Xu Minghong (1897–1934) was the Nineteenth Route Army’s secretary-general and a secret Communist, and it was he who negotiated the army’s anti-Japanese accords with Pan Hannian. After the Fujian revolt collapsed he was captured and executed by the Kuomintang in 1934 — the death Liang Shuming mourns below.

The China Weekly Review (Chinese Milei-shi Pinglun-bao, after its American founder Thomas Millard) was Shanghai’s leading English-language weekly, an influential voice on Chinese affairs from 1917 into the 1950s.

ch11.anchor: to resist the outside one must first pacify within
ch11.note: “To resist the outside, first pacify within” (rangwai bi xian annei) was Chiang Kai-shek’s governing slogan of the early 1930s: crush the Communists at home before confronting Japan. It was why he would not back the very resistance to Japan that the Nineteenth Route Army was waging.

ch11.anchor: lending his voice to the "Gongche petition,"
ch11.note: The “Gongche petition” of 1895 — named for the post-carriages that had once carried tribute candidates to the capital — was the mass memorial by examination candidates, led by Kang Youwei and Liang Qichao, that protested the treaty ending the war with Japan and demanded reform. It launched the constitutional-reform movement the young Yang Du joined.

Red Flag Weekly (Hongqi Zhoubao) was a central organ of the CCP, published clandestinely in Shanghai from 1931. That Yang Du brushed its masthead is one of the recurring proofs offered, throughout this section, for his secret Party tie.

Qi Baishi (1864–1957), whose original name was Qi Huang, was the most celebrated Chinese painter of the twentieth century, famous above all for his ink studies of shrimp, insects, plants and small creatures.

ch11.anchor: the Annamese patrolmen dare not touch it
ch11.note: The French Concession recruited many of its police in French Indochina; these “Annamese” (Vietnamese) patrolmen answered to the French authorities, so a house under Du Yuesheng’s protection there lay beyond the reach of the Chinese police and the International Settlement’s alike.

Xibaipo, a village in Hebei, was the seat of the CCP Central Committee in 1948–49, on the eve of victory; from it Mao Zedong and Zhou Enlai directed the closing campaigns of the civil war and received prospective allies, as here.

ch11.anchor: the editors of the Cihai in Shanghai
ch11.note: The Cihai (“Sea of Words”) is the standard large encyclopedic dictionary of Chinese, compiled and published in Shanghai; an entry in it carries a quasi-official authority, which is why Zhou Enlai wanted Yang Du’s Party membership set down there.

The China Relief Society (Zhongguo Huji Zonghui), founded in 1930, was a Communist-led body that raised money and legal aid for arrested revolutionaries and their families; Song Qingling and Lu Xun were among its public sponsors.

In July 1917 the Qing loyalist general Zhang Xun briefly put the boy emperor Puyi back on the throne in Beijing; the coup collapsed within days. It was this fiasco, Yang Du says, that finally convinced him monarchy was hopeless.
The source prints jiangjun (“generals”) where the sense is plainly Jiang jun, “Chiang’s army”: 150,000 Nationalist troops, not 150,000 generals. Rendered here to the meaning. [—Trans.]

Zhang Yufa (b. 1936) is a leading historian of modern China at Taiwan’s Academia Sinica. The author gives him the last, skeptical word: that Yang Du’s late service to the CCP may have been less a conversion than one more turn of a lifelong gift for playing every side at once.

ch12.anchor: Sun Qi's Records of the Northern Ward
ch12.note: Records of the Northern Ward (Beili zhi) is a late-Tang account by Sun Qi of the Ping’kang ward, the licensed courtesans’ quarter in the north of the capital, Chang’an. From it beili, “the northern ward,” passed into literary Chinese as a standing byword for the brothel district — the sense the newspaper report plays on here.
Ni Zan (1301–1374), one of the Four Masters of the Yuan, celebrated for spare, tranquil ink landscapes of rock, water and a few bare trees. The source names him by his sobriquet Ni Yu.

ch12.anchor: the lewd music of Zheng and Wei
ch12.note: In the Confucian classics the songs of the ancient states of Zheng and Wei were the byword for licentious, morally loosening music, set against the upright music of the sages; “the sounds of Zheng” is a standard figure for corrupting art. Qian Huafo uses it to say the Little Garden had sunk wholly into vice.

The “Noulens” couple — Hilaire Noulens (a cover name of Yakov Rudnik) and his wife — were Comintern liaison agents in Shanghai. Their arrest in June 1931 laid bare much of the Comintern’s Far Eastern network; an international campaign to save them, joined by Song Qingling and Smedley, failed. Their case threads through this book’s intelligence story.

ch12.anchor: Yang Xingfo and others got wind
ch12.note: Yang Xingfo (Yang Quan, 1893–1933), a US-trained scholar and administrator, secretary-general of the Academia Sinica and executive secretary of the Civil Rights League. Blue Shirt gunmen assassinated him in Shanghai on June 18, 1933, on the steps of the Academia Sinica — the killing recounted later in this chapter.

ch12.anchor: through the China League for the Protection of Civil Rights
ch12.note: The China League for the Protection of Civil Rights (Zhongguo minquan baozhang tongmeng), a civil-liberties body founded in Shanghai in December 1932 under Song Qingling, with Cai Yuanpei, Lu Xun and Yang Xingfo. It campaigned for the release of political prisoners; after Yang Xingfo’s assassination in June 1933 it effectively ceased to exist.

Agnes Smedley (1892–1950), American radical journalist and author of the autobiographical novel Daughter of Earth. A committed supporter of the Chinese Communists, she reported from China through the 1930s. Her recollections here are a partisan witness’s; the author sets them against the contemporary newspaper record below and finds them wrong on several points.

ch12.anchor: the young American reporter Harold Isaacs
ch12.note: Harold Isaacs (1910–1986), American journalist then in Shanghai, where he edited the left-wing China Forum; later the author of The Tragedy of the Chinese Revolution (1938), a classic account written from a dissident-left standpoint.

ch12.anchor: Lin Yutang, Lu Xun and others were on the executive
ch12.note: Lin Yutang (1895–1976), essayist and editor, at this time an officer of the Civil Rights League; a few years later, with My Country and My People (1935), he became the best-known interpreter of China to English-speaking readers.

ch12.anchor: Hu Shi, too, in his *Independent Critic*
ch12.note: Hu Shi (1891–1962), the foremost liberal intellectual of Republican China and a champion of writing in the vernacular; his weekly the Independent Critic (Duli pinglun) ran from 1932. Printing the mayor’s flat denial places him here on the government’s side of the case — a stance the League’s people held against him.

The Blue Shirts Society (Lanyishe), a secret ultranationalist paramilitary formed within the Kuomintang in 1932 on an avowedly fascist model, used for surveillance, intimidation and political murder. Its gunmen carried out Yang Xingfo’s assassination.
L’Impartial (Da Gong Bao), a leading independent Chinese daily founded in Tianjin in 1902; the French title was the paper’s own.

ch12.anchor: a well-known poet of the Lakeside school
ch12.note: The Lakeside Poetry Society (Hupan), founded at Hangzhou’s West Lake in 1922 by Ying Xiuren, Wang Jingzhi and others, known for fresh, direct love-lyrics. Ying Xiuren was one of its founders.

The Mukden, or September 18, Incident of 1931: the Japanese Kwantung Army’s staged pretext for seizing Manchuria. It set off the scattered anti-Japanese volunteer resistance in the Northeast mentioned here.

Jiang Boyue is Jiang Wei (202–264), the last great general of Shu Han. After his state fell he feigned surrender to the conquering Wei in a bid to restore it from within; the plot was found out and he was killed. Meng Huating means their own feigned surrender has come to the same ruin.

ch13.anchor: the food of Aphrodite, the goddess of love
ch13.note: The chapter opens with a passage from the memoirs of Isadora Duncan (1877–1927), the American dancer who pioneered a free, expressive style against the formality of classical ballet. The young Shen Anna helped translate Duncan’s autobiography into Chinese in 1934, and its cadences run through the whole chapter, which closes on Duncan again. Aphrodite is the Greek goddess of love and beauty, to whom oysters and champagne were reckoned sacred.

ch13.anchor: Shen Wan became an intelligence agent
ch13.note: Shen Anna (1915–2010), born Shen Wan, became one of the most durable agents in the history of Chinese Communist intelligence. A trained stenographer, she took the minutes at the Kuomintang’s most secret meetings for some fourteen years, from 1938 into 1949, and fed the record to the Party; she was later called “the Red stenographer.” She and her husband, Hua Mingzhi, worked as a married pair, the “twin lotus” of the chapter’s title. Her memoir, cited here as (Shen Anna, 2016), is an interested witness to her own life; where it can be checked it is broadly corroborated.

Nakanishi Ko (1910–1973) was a Japanese communist who worked for the Comintern and the Chinese Communist Party, gathering intelligence inside Japanese official circles in China; arrested by the Japanese in 1942 and sentenced to death, he survived the war. The record of his interrogation is used here as a source on Wang Xuewen’s intelligence role.

ch13.anchor: the Chinese Workers' and Peasants' Red Army Vanguard Column
ch13.note: In the winter of 1934–35 the Red Army’s Anti-Japanese Vanguard, sent into Fujian and Zhejiang to draw pressure off the main Long March, was trapped and destroyed at Mount Huaiyu. Its survivors, some four hundred men under Su Yu and Liu Ying, regrouped as the Advance Column (tingjinshi, rendered “Vanguard Column” here) and waged a guerrilla war across the Zhejiang mountains from 1935 until the united front of 1937. The account follows standard PRC military histories.

ch13.anchor: Su Yu as military-region chief of staff
ch13.note: Su Yu (1907–1984) rose from these guerrilla years to become one of the Communist side’s ablest field commanders, winning the great Huaihai campaign of 1948–49; he was made a general in 1955.

Fang Zhimin (1899–1935), the Communist leader of the Fujian–Zhejiang–Jiangxi base, was captured after Mount Huaiyu and executed at Nanchang on August 6, 1935. In prison he wrote the essay Lovable China, long a staple of Communist patriotic reading. His death is well attested.

ch13.anchor: the Marco Polo Bridge Incident broke out
ch13.note: The clash at the Marco Polo Bridge (Lugouqiao), just outside Beiping, on July 7, 1937, opened the full-scale war between China and Japan that lasted until 1945, and is often taken as the start of the Second World War in Asia.
“August Thirteenth” is the Battle of Shanghai, which began on August 13, 1937, when heavy fighting engulfed the city; it scattered the Communist underground there and cut Shen Anna’s link to it.

ch13.anchor: to ask Zhu Jiahua to arrange work for her
ch13.note: Zhu Jiahua (1893–1963), a German-trained geologist, president of the Academia Sinica, and a senior Kuomintang administrator, was at this time secretary-general of the party’s Central Headquarters. His patronage, extended to a former subordinate, put Shen Anna inside the Kuomintang’s confidential secretariat, the pivot on which this chapter turns.

The Southern Anhui Incident of January 1941, known in the West as the New Fourth Army Incident, was a Kuomintang attack on the headquarters column of the Communists’ New Fourth Army; several thousand were killed or captured. It marked the near-collapse of the united front and the hardening anti-Communist line these documents record, and is amply corroborated.

Yan Baohang (1895–1968) was a Christian social reformer who moved in high Kuomintang and diplomatic circles while secretly working for the Communists; his intelligence is credited with warning Moscow of the timing of the German invasion of the Soviet Union in 1941. His son Yan Mingfu later held senior Party posts.

ch13.anchor: volume sixty of the Draft Chronicle
ch13.note: The Draft Chronicle (Shilue Gaoben) is the vast day-by-day compilation of Chiang Kai-shek’s papers, orders, and movements kept by his secretariat, and one of the principal primary sources for his career. The author sets its private record beside the Kuomintang’s internal directives to argue a settled anti-Communist purpose behind the public talk of a “political solution.”

ch13.anchor: three years without a sale, then one sale feeds you three years
ch13.note: A shopkeepers’ saying, of a trade so slow that a single big sale must carry the business for years, here a wry salute to the couple’s three barren years and the windfall haul of Kuomintang secrets that ended them.
A Shanghai turn of phrase for people who take a table at a dance hall but never dance, as idle and fixed in place as a fortune-teller waiting at his sidewalk stall for custom.

ch13.anchor: the greatest image has no form
ch13.note: These lines are from the Daodejing (chapter 41): “The greatest white seems soiled ... the greatest note is faint of sound, the greatest image has no form” — the highest things go unseen and unheard, a fitting emblem for a life spent invisible. The two phrases before them are a maxim on guarding the tongue and the Confucian ideal of “watchfulness when alone” (shendu).

The maxim that follows — sow an act and reap a habit, a habit and a character, a character and a destiny — circulates widely in English and has been attributed to many hands, among them the novelist Charles Reade and the writer Samuel Smiles; it is not securely the work of any philosopher, and “Pudeman” cannot be matched to a known name. Rendered here as the source prints it. [—Trans.]

The chapter’s title, “Twin Lotus on One Stem” (bingdilian), names two lotus blossoms that open on a single stalk, a classical Chinese image for a devoted married couple. Here it is doubled and literal: two married pairs, Shen Anna with Hua Mingzhi and, in Shanghai, her sister with Shu Yuexin, each couple a working intelligence cell.

ch14.anchor: had once presented to a courtesan.
ch14.note: The bawdy couplet that follows strings together stock tropes for a famous beauty: a glance that “topples a city” and “topples a kingdom” echoes a Han-dynasty ode to the beauty Lady Li; the promise to “keep her in a house of gold” recalls the boy emperor Wu of Han, who vowed to house his cousin Ah Jiao in a golden chamber; and to “breed dragons and serpents” is to bear extraordinary sons.

ch14.anchor: worth recruiting as one of their own.
ch14.note: Luo Zhanglong (1896–1995), one of the earliest Communist labor leaders, broke with the leadership over the Fourth Plenum of 1931 and was expelled from the Party; the bitterness of that break colors the venomous memoir quoted here (see Chapter Nine). The nicknames he uses are decoded two lines down.

ch14.anchor: 'nine-tailed turtles' of the ten-li foreign quarter,"
ch14.note: A “nine-tailed turtle” (jiuwei gui) was Shanghai slang for a rich philanderer and habitué of brothels, after the hugely popular late-Qing novel of that name (1906), whose dandy hero comes to grief in the pleasure quarters.

ch14.anchor: the "Secret Number One" of our Party's early memory.
ch14.note: The Central Archive (Zhongyang Wenku) was the Communist Party’s first secret document repository. The chapter that follows tells how a chain of keepers preserved its more than twenty thousand items intact through nearly two decades of terror, war, and occupation; the collection was handed over whole in 1949 and entered the Central Archives in Beijing in 1959. Its survival is among the most celebrated feats of the underground.

The Fifth Plenum of the Kuomintang’s Central Executive Committee, in January 1939, marked Chiang Kai-shek’s turn from the united front toward containing the Communists; it adopted the “Measures for Restricting the Activities of Alien Parties,” the policy this Party directive is denouncing.

ch14.anchor: executive member of the "China Defence League")
ch14.note: The China Defence League, founded in Hong Kong in 1938 by Song Qingling (Madame Sun Yat-sen), raised money and medical supplies abroad for China’s resistance and steered much of the aid to the Communist areas.

Kong Xiangxi (1881–1967), known in the West as H. H. Kung, was a banker, Nationalist finance minister and premier, and—through his wife Soong Ai-ling—a brother-in-law of both Chiang Kai-shek and Sun Yat-sen. That a Communist agent sat among his advisers shows how deep the penetration ran.

ch14.anchor: confessed to Section 1 of the Tokkō of the Japanese Metropolitan Police Board
ch14.note: The Tokkō (Tokubetsu Kōtō Keisatsu, the “Special Higher Police”) was Japan’s political and thought police, charged with suppressing communists, dissidents, and spies; Section 1 of its Tokyo headquarters conducted the interrogations in this case.

“Ramsay” was the cover name of Richard Sorge (introduced in Chapter Seven), the Soviet military-intelligence officer whose ring in Tokyo warned Moscow that Japan would strike south at the United States, not north at the USSR—intelligence that let Stalin shift his Far Eastern divisions west. This Japan-based ring was separate from the CCP’s Shanghai net but exchanged intelligence with it through Nakanishi. The author’s arrest dates just below run a day or two later than the standard record (Ozaki was taken on October 14, 1941).

ch14.anchor: "Comintern espionage ring" affair, beginning the arrests in June 1942.
ch14.note: The affair the Japanese called the “Comintern espionage ring” rolled up a network of Japanese Communists working for the CCP and the Comintern from inside Japanese institutions in China. Its chief figures were Nakanishi (see Chapter Thirteen), an analyst in the South Manchuria Railway’s research arm, and Nishizato Tatsuo, a correspondent of the Dōmei news agency; both were arrested in 1942 and sentenced to death, and both survived the war.

No. 51 Depot (1961) is a classic film of the underground war, in which a New Fourth Army officer runs a secret supply station in occupied Shanghai in the guise of “the Little Boss,” the protégé of a gangland chief. Miao Guren’s cover as a businessman smuggling medicine to the Communist forces is the real-life counterpart.

ch14.anchor: Zheng Wendao was "great in life, glorious in death."
ch14.note: “Great in life, glorious in death” (sheng de weida, si de guangrong) is Mao Zedong’s celebrated 1947 inscription for Liu Hulan, a fifteen-year-old villager executed by Nationalist troops; the author lends the most famous of all Communist martyr-epitaphs to Zheng Wendao.

ch15.anchor: deputy general manager of the Zhejiang Industrial Bank
ch15.note: Zhang Naiqi was a prominent banker and essayist. He later became one of the “Seven Gentlemen” of the National Salvation Association, arrested by the Nationalists in 1936 for pressing for resistance to Japan, and after 1949 served as the People’s Republic’s first minister of food.

ch15.anchor: Beishanxi Road, in the International Settlement.
ch15.note: So printed in the source, here and again just below. There was no “Beishanxi Road” in the Shanghai settlements; the name is almost certainly a slip for Shanxi North Road, a street in the northern part of the International Settlement.—Trans.

ch15.anchor: when Kirov, a member of the Politburo of the Soviet Communist Party, was assassinated
ch15.note: Sergei Kirov, the Leningrad party chief and a member of the Soviet Politburo, was shot dead on December 1, 1934. Stalin used the killing as the pretext for the terror that became the Great Purge, in which the hunt for alleged “Trotskyists” swept up Soviet and foreign Communists alike, the Chinese students in Moscow among them.

Georgi Dimitrov (1882–1949), the Bulgarian Communist who had won worldwide fame by turning his own defense at the 1933 Reichstag-fire trial in Nazi Germany into an indictment of the Nazis, was elected general secretary of the Comintern at its Seventh Congress in 1935. He became the public face of its new line of a broad united front against fascism.

The “August First Declaration” marked the CCP’s public turn from the class-war line of the soviet years toward a national united front against Japan. Issued in the name of the Chinese Soviet government and the Party Center, it was in fact drafted by the CCP delegation in Moscow around the time of the Comintern’s Seventh Congress, and it prefigured the second Nationalist–Communist alliance of 1937.

ch15.anchor: brothers who quarrel within the walls still join to repel insult from without
ch15.note: An allusion to the Book of Songs (Shijing): “Brothers may quarrel within the walls, yet outside they defend one another against insult.” The classical line is invoked to urge Nationalists and Communists to set aside their civil war and unite against the Japanese.

The source names the Western agent only as “Walton,” a transliteration of the Chinese Hua’erdun; his identity is not established here. The 1935 prosecution belongs to the wave of trials of Comintern and Soviet military-intelligence networks in China that had begun with the arrest of the Noulens couple in 1931 (see Chapter Twelve).

Chen Yun’s account, written under the pen name “Lianchen” and cast as the notes of a captured doctor traveling with the Red Army, was the first substantial insider narrative of the Long March to reach the outside world; it appeared in the Communist Chinese press in Paris and Moscow in 1936.

“Zhu-Mao” joins the names of Zhu De, the Red Army’s commander-in-chief, and Mao Zedong, its political leader. From the late 1920s the two were so bound up with the force that outsiders sometimes took “Zhu Mao” for the name of a single man.

ch15.anchor: today it has become a prairie fire
ch15.note: An echo of Mao Zedong’s celebrated 1930 essay, whose title is usually given in English as “A Single Spark Can Start a Prairie Fire” (from the classical saying that a single spark can set the whole plain ablaze).

ch00.anchor: a keynote address to the mobilization meeting for the study of Party history
ch00.note: Xi Jinping, general secretary of the Chinese Communist Party and China’s paramount leader, launched a nationwide “Party history study and education” campaign in early 2021, the year of the Party’s centenary. He frames the whole book with this speech; the celebratory, embattled register of the pages that follow belongs to that political moment as much as to the story.—Trans.

In 2009, for the sixtieth anniversary of the People’s Republic, a national poll chose one hundred “heroes and models who made outstanding contributions to the founding of New China” and one hundred “figures who moved China” in the years since 1949; the two lists together were called the “Double Hundred.”

Not the Tang poet of the same name. Li Bai (1910–1949) was a Communist wireless operator in Shanghai, arrested and, days before the city fell to the Communists in 1949, executed by the Nationalists. His story was the basis for the celebrated 1958 film The Unfailing Radio Waves and the later ballet of the same name.

ch00.anchor: the roll of the "Three Heroes of Longtan"
ch00.note: The “Three Heroes of Longtan” (Longtan means “Dragon Pool”) were Qian Zhuangfei, Li Kenong, and Hu Di, the three Communists who penetrated the Nationalists’ own intelligence apparatus. In April 1931 their warning saved the Party’s Shanghai leadership after Gu Shunzhang defected; their story is told in Chapter Eight.

ch00.anchor: His Real Work Was to Lurk
ch00.note: The verb renders 潜伏, “to lie hidden,” to go undercover, which is also the title of Lurk (2008–2009), a hugely popular Chinese television drama about a Communist mole inside Nationalist intelligence. The pun sets the actor-grandfather’s screen roles against his real underground work.

Qian Jiang (1918–1994), Qian Zhuangfei’s son, was one of the People’s Republic’s most celebrated cinematographers; the films named here—Daughters of China, The White-Haired Girl, New Year Sacrifice, The Lin Family Shop, and Hai Xia—are classics of Chinese cinema. His documentary reportage Seven Top-Secret Telegrams lay behind the 1985 film A Nanjing Night.

A sensationalized 1996 account of Communist intelligence work, which the author holds up as the opposite of his own method; the passages he quotes turn the defector Gu Shunzhang into a lurid pulp hero.—Trans.

Gu Shunzhang, the Central Special Branch’s chief of operations, was the Party’s most damaging defector; his surrender to the Nationalists in April 1931 nearly destroyed the underground leadership (see Chapters Six through Eight). The real episode the author invokes—Gu escorting senior cadres to the Hubei-Henan-Anhui (E-Yu-Wan) base area, one of the largest Communist rural soviets—is, he complains, rewritten here as pulp fiction.
An earlier book by the author, Minguo Yi’an (2008), on unsolved criminal and political cases of the Republican period (1912–1949).

ch00.anchor: History is not a little girl to be dressed up as one pleases.
ch00.note: An inversion of a famous line—“history is a little girl anyone can dress up as they please”—popularly attributed to the scholar Hu Shi, though he never wrote it in that form. In Chinese arguments over “historical nihilism” the saying stands for the cynical view that the past can be made to mean anything; the author turns it on its head.

ch00.anchor: riches and honor cannot corrupt, poverty and low station cannot move, force and arms cannot bend
ch00.note: From the Mencius (3rd century BCE), the classic Chinese definition of the great man: one whom “riches and honor cannot corrupt, poverty and low station cannot move, force and arms cannot bend.”

ch00.anchor: the five martyrs of the League of Left-Wing Writers
ch00.note: Five young left-wing writers—Rou Shi, Yin Fu, Hu Yepin, Feng Keng, and Li Weisen—arrested and secretly shot by the Nationalists at Longhua, on the edge of Shanghai, on February 7, 1931. Lu Xun was close to several of them.
Lu Xun’s essay Wei le wangque de jinian (1933), written to mourn the five and to defy the silence around them; the closing lines paraphrased here are among the most quoted in modern Chinese prose.

ch00.anchor: oppose historical nihilism under a clear banner
ch00.note: “Historical nihilism” (lishi xuwu zhuyi) is an official term in the People’s Republic for accounts that question the received, celebratory version of Party history; combating it has been a stated aim of state cultural policy under Xi Jinping. The author writes squarely from within that campaign.—Trans.

ch00.anchor: the Sixth National Security Education Day for All
ch00.note: April 15 was designated China’s annual National Security Education Day under the 2015 National Security Law; 2021 was the sixth. The date of the author’s signature is itself a statement of the book’s theme.—Trans.

ch17.anchor: Shen Anna, died in Beijing at the age of ninety-five
ch17.note: Shen Anna (1915–2010), born Shen Wan, was the Communists’ long-planted stenographer inside the Nationalist high command, taking down its most secret conferences in shorthand for more than a decade; her story, and that of her husband Hua Mingzhi, is told in Chapter Thirteen.

The people named in this long paragraph are the children, grandchildren, and other kin of the Central Special Branch figures the book has told of—among them Zhou Enlai, Chen Yun, Bo Gu, Chen Geng, Li Kenong, Qian Zhuangfei, Pan Hannian, and Dong Jianwu—whom the author consulted while researching it.

ch17.anchor: This too I learned from Mr. Yang Tianshi.
ch17.note: Yang Tianshi (b. 1936) is one of China’s most eminent historians of the Republican period, a research fellow of the Institute of Modern History at the Chinese Academy of Social Sciences, and best known abroad for his work on Chiang Kai-shek’s diaries.

ch17.anchor: To know what you know and to know what you do not know
ch17.note: From the Analects of Confucius: “When you know a thing, to hold that you know it; and when you do not know a thing, to allow that you do not know it—this is knowledge.”

The Yanshi Jiaxun (Family Instructions for the Yan Clan), written in the sixth century by Yan Zhitui, is the earliest surviving Chinese book of family precepts; its chapter “Exhortation to Study” is a classic statement of scholarly caution. The “correcting brush” renders cihuang, orpiment, the yellow mineral once painted over a manuscript to blot out and amend a character.
